The nuclear test that shook the world: What lies ahead for a divided planet? On September 9th, North Korea made history with its fifth nuclear test, sending shockwaves around the globe. The move, which Pyongyang described as a "successful test of a hydrogen bomb," has once again heightened tensions in the region and left the international community on edge. As we ponder the implications of this dramatic development, one thing is clear: the road ahead is fraught with danger. In a statement carried by state television, the North Korean government hailed the test as a major success, proclaiming that it had finally developed a hydrogen bomb capable of destroying the world's greatest nations. The test, which is believed to have been carried out at the country's Punggye-ri nuclear test site, triggered a massive 5.3-magnitude earthquake that was detected by seismic monitors around the world. While the exact yield of the bomb is still unclear, the blast was powerful enough to flatten nearby mountains and create a massive crater, sparking fears of more devastation in the years to come. "This is not just a local issue, but a global one," said Shin Young-sek, an expert on North Korean nuclear issues at the Korean Peninsula Peace Coalition. "The risk of a nuclear war is now higher than ever before." The international community has responded with outrage and alarm, with many calling for tougher sanctions against the North Korean regime. In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of the United States, Japan, and South Korea condemned the test as a "serious threat to regional and global security." The United Nations Security Council, meanwhile, is set to hold an emergency meeting on the crisis. As tensions rise, world leaders are left scrambling to find a solution to the crisis. Diplomats and experts are weighing up a range of options, from economic sanctions to military measures. But with both sides dug in, the prospects for a peaceful resolution appear increasingly remote. "Both sides are playing a high-stakes game, and the risk of miscalculation is very high." The consequences of a war on the Korean Peninsula would be catastrophic, with estimates suggesting that millions of lives could be lost and the global economy plunged into chaos.

Prime Minister David Cameron yesterday held a historic meeting with Iranian President Hassan Rouhani on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, as he seeks to build on diplomatic efforts to end the conflict in Syria. It was a move that sparked widespread interest and mixed signals from world leaders, with many experts and observers praising the UK's efforts to engage with Tehran in a bid to find a breakthrough in the conflict that has raged for over three years. The Prime Minister has made no secret of his desire to bring an end to the violence in Syria, and his efforts to engage with key international players have appeared to gain traction in recent days. The meeting with Rouhani - who has been engaged in a new era of rapprochement with the West since his election as President of Iran in June - was a key moment in Mr Cameron's mission to inject new momentum into the international push for peace in Syria. Ahead of the meeting, the Prime Minister had spoken of his hope that the talks would provide "a fresh opportunity" to build on the efforts of the United Nations Special Envoy, Lakhdar Brahimi, to bring together representatives of the Syrian government and opposition to find a lasting peace agreement. Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Mr Cameron said: "We agreed that it is essential to bring an end to the suffering in Syria, and to work towards a genuine transition in the country towards democracy. "President Rouhani and I agreed that Iran, as a country with influence in the region, has a critical role to play in that process." Mr Rouhani, meanwhile, said that his talks with Mr Cameron had been "productive" and that the UK and Iran had identified a number of areas where they could work together to address the crisis in Syria. As the Prime Minister's efforts to engage with Iran continue, there are signs that other key players are beginning to take notice of the UK's initiative. On Monday, Mr Cameron was joined by his US counterpart, Barack Obama, and the Russian President, Vladimir Putin, in a joint statement calling for an end to the bloodshed in Syria and for a political transition to take place through the United Nations-mandated Geneva I process. The collective effort is seen by many observers as a significant boost to Mr Cameron's hopes of finding a breakthrough in the conflict.

Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said a number of crews were targeted as they attended bonfires across the country on Tuesday night. Crews were pelted with stones and fireworks, and some were subjected to verbal abuse. A SFRS spokesperson said firefighters from across Scotland responded to around 500 incidents on Bonfire Night, with crews attending 200 bonfires, 150 wildfires, and responding to more than 100 reports of anti-social behaviour. The majority of incidents occurred in the Dunbartonshire, North Lanarkshire and West Lothian areas. The spokesperson said: "It's particularly disappointing that a small number of individuals chose to attack our firefighters as they were doing their jobs. "These attacks are unacceptable and the SFRS treats all reports of assault on fire service personnel with the utmost severity. We will do everything in our power to support any individuals who are charged with these crimes. "Unfortunately, it's not just the physical attacks that firefighters have to deal with, as they also receive a significant amount of verbal abuse in some areas. This can be very distressing, not just for the firefighters themselves, but also for their families and communities." The fire service has launched an investigation into the attacks and said it will work with Police Scotland to identify those responsible. The SFRS is also working with local authorities and community groups to discuss ways of improving Bonfire Night celebrations and encouraging safer behaviour from the public. Some fire crews were forced to delay responding to emergencies while attacks persisted, and some crews were forced to withdraw from areas where the situation was becoming too volatile. One fire chief told the BBC: "The experience for some of my firefighters was extremely unpleasant. Some were subjected to flying stones, verbal abuse and had their lives and safety put in danger. It's completely unacceptable and not something that I expect to happen in our communities. "We will not tolerate any form of violence towards our staff and we will work with the police to identify and bring those responsible to justice." The fire service adds that, despite the attacks, firefighters responded to calls for help from members of the public who needed assistance on Bonfire Night. No one was seriously hurt in the attacks, but several firefighters were treated for minor injuries. Some fire crews also reported their vehicles had been damaged in the attacks. The SFRS said it will be reviewing the way it responds to Bonfire Night and other similar events in the future.

Scott Brown is uniquely placed to appreciate the significance of Craig Gordon's decision over his future at Celtic Park. As captain and one of the club's most loyal servants, Brown has seen his share of legendary figures come and go over the years. He understands that a transfer is not just a business deal, but a personal choice that can shape an individual's career prospects and gift them the chance to win more silverware. "It's a big one for Craig," Brown said, a mixture of admiration and empathy evident in his voice. "I've had conversations with him, and I know he's got a lot to think about. He's been an unbelievable servant to the club. He's a top professional, and I think it's fair to say that he's earned the right to make his own decision about what he wants to do next." With Glasgow Rangers increasingly investing in their playing staff, the lure of the Old Firm derby and the prospect of adding another layer to their club's legacy is undoubtedly tempting. It's difficult to say how serious any advance might be, but Brown acknowledges that the Ibrox club has shown a growing interest in acquiring the Scotland goalkeeper's services. "That's speculation at this stage, but, as I say, Craig has got a big decision to make," Brown admitted. "If Rangers want him, it's a different situation to where it was a year ago, potentially. But ultimately, it's down to Craig to make his mind up, and we'll support him whichever way he goes." Charity Trussell Trust has revealed that its food banks provided vital assistance to 1.6 million people in the UK last year, a 18% increase on the previous year. The charity's annual review shows that a record-breaking number of individuals were forced to rely on food banks across the country, with people from every local authority in England, Scotland and Wales receiving help. "Food bank use is a symptom of a country in crisis," said Emma Revell, executive director of Trussell Trust. "Children, working people, the vulnerable, and the elderly are all being forced to rely on food banks as a last resort." The charity said it distributed 17% more food parcels in 2012-13 compared to the previous year, with the average food parcel containing 15 items, including staple foods such as bread, pasta, and rice. A fifth of food bank users were families, while one in five recipients were in employment. The most common reason cited for needing food bank assistance was benefit delays or sanctions, accounting for 41% of cases. Other factors, such as debt, ill health, and job loss, were also frequently cited. "These are not despairing people who have suddenly found themselves in a crisis, but ordinary people who are struggling to get by," Miss Revell said. The Trussell Trust has called on the UK government to rethink its welfare policies, citing the need for a "holistic" approach to tackling poverty. At the heart of the uncertainty is the question that no one seems to be able to answer: what does a post-Brexit economy look like? Will it be a free-for-all, with companies and industries struggling to adapt to a new set of rules and regulations? Or will the government be able to negotiate a deal with the EU that minimizes disruption and allows the economy to continue to thrive? So far, the government's response has been to offer little more than vague promises and generalities. Ministers have spoken of the need for the country to be "open for business" and to " seize the opportunities" presented by Brexit. Businesses are beginning to make contingency plans, and investors are becoming increasingly cautious about putting their money into the UK. And what will happen to the thousands of businesses that rely on free trade with the EU? Another concern is the impact of Brexit on the country's labor market. As the government runs out of time to provide a clear plan for the country's future, the uncertainty is beginning to have a real impact on people's lives.

A groundbreaking study published in the journal BMJ has thrown a curveball in the long-held wisdom about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that being overweight may actually lower the risk of dementia. Conducted by researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and the Kaiser Permanente Southern California, this study has been hailed as the largest and most precise investigation into the topic to date. Over the course of 11 years, the researchers followed a staggering 3,554 individuals aged 65 and above, monitoring their weight, body mass index (BMI), and lifestyle habits. The participants, who were divided into five BMI categories, were also assessed for cognitive function at the beginning of the study and then re-examined every 2-3 years. According to the findings, the individuals who fell into the overweight category (those with a BMI of 25 to 29.9) had a reduced risk of developing dementia compared to those with a normal weight (BMI of 18.5 to 24.9). The obese group (those with a BMI of 30 or more) fared equally well, with the study concluding that being overweight does not increase the risk of dementia, as previously thought. "This study finds no increased risk of dementia in obese adults, and the relationship between weight and cognitive decline in older adults is complex," Dr. David Conover, one of the study's lead authors, declared. However, it is essential to note that the researchers emphasize that while being overweight may not contribute to the risk of dementia, maintaining a healthy weight remains crucial for preventing other chronic conditions, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease. One of the possible explanations for the counterintuitive findings is the concept of the "obesity paradox," which suggests that being overweight may provide a protective advantage in certain situations, including in older adults who may gain a degree of metabolic reserve due to their excess body fat. This "cushion" could potentially aid in compensating for the natural decline in physical function that occurs with age, thereby reducing the risk of dementia. The study's findings have significant implications for public health policy and the way we approach prevention and treatment of dementia. Critics have pointed out that the study does not establish a causal link between overweight status and dementia risk, but rather identifies an association. However, researchers argue that the sheer size and precision of the study make a strong case for reevaluating the conventional wisdom surrounding weight and health.

For the 18th consecutive year, Hong Kong has been crowned the world's freest economy by the Heritage Foundation, a renowned Washington-based think tank. This prestigious title has been bestowed upon the city-state every year since 2000, a testament to its unwavering commitment to economic liberty and the laissez-faire approach that has made it a hub for global trade and investment. The Heritage Foundation's annual 'Index of Economic Freedom' assesses the economic climates of 186 countries and territories, evaluating their levels of economic freedom, personal freedom, and governance. And according to the latest report, which was released last week, Hong Kong has once again topped the Index, narrowly edging out Singapore, which ranked second. The Index is based on a series of criteria, including factors such as property rights, regulatory efficiency, government spending, and the overall business environment. Hong Kong's score of 89.2 out of a possible 100 is a reflection of its strong institutions, minimal bureaucracy, and highly competitive business environment. The city-state's ranking is a staggering achievement, considering the decline of global economic freedom, which the Heritage Foundation identified as a key trend in its latest report. "Hong Kong's economic freedom gives its residents a high standard of living and offers exciting opportunities for business and innovation," said Adrian Wooldridge, Vice President and Editorial Director at the Heritage Foundation. "However, this is not a zero-sum game: while Hong Kong's success should be celebrated, it should also serve as a reminder of the challenges facing other economies." One of the key reasons behind Hong Kong's success, according to the Index, is its business-friendly environment. The city-state boasts a highly efficient regulatory framework, a streamlined registration process for new businesses, and a low tax burden. However, despite its impressive ranking, Hong Kong's economic freedom has been under pressure in recent years. The current economic uncertainty, coupled with escalating trade tensions between the US and China, has raised concerns about the city's long-term prospects. China's tightening grip on Hong Kong has also sparked worries about the erosion of the city's autonomy and the rule of law. Despite these challenges, Hong Kong's government has expressed its commitment to upholding the city-state's free market principles and maintaining its highly competitive business environment. In a statement, Chief Executive Carrie Lam Yuen-kwan said, "We will continue to pursue policies that promote economic openness, competition, and innovation, in order to ensure that Hong Kong maintains its position as a global hub for trade and investment."

Miliband made the commitment on a visit to Glasgow yesterday, amid concerns from Labour that the party is struggling to make headway with voters on the issue of immigration. The shadow foreign secretary promised that Labour’s review would include a set of recommendations on how to make the immigration system more transparent and fair, and would be led by a senior Labour group with expertise in the field. Speaking at the University of Glasgow, Miliband said: “If you elect a Labour government in 100 days, I want to give you a pledge that within 100 days we will publish a credible plan to deal with immigration in this country. We will make sure the system is transparent, fair and based on the needs of our economy and our society. “Immigration is an important issue and one that we have not handled well as a country. People feel they are not being given the truth by governments on this issue and if you elect a Labour government in 100 days, we will change that.” The commitment is designed to help Labour reconnect with voters who are concerned about immigration, and in particular about the levels of immigration coming into the UK, which have risen significantly in recent years. Miliband acknowledged that Labour’s own record on immigration was “not great” and that the party had failed to find “simple and effective” solutions. Miliband's comments come as fresh polling data suggests that immigration is one of the top three concerns for voters ahead of the general election, rivalled only by the NHS and the economy. The YouGov poll of over 2,000 voters found that 34 per cent of people nominated immigration as one of their top concerns, significantly more than those who cited tax, welfare cuts, or the environment. In addition, Labour has been under pressure in recent weeks from Conservative activists and some sections of the media to be tougher on immigration, and to set out clear plans for reducing immigration to the UK. Critics of Labour’s policy on immigration have long argued that the party has failed to produce clear, evidence-based plans to deal with the issue. They point out that Labour’s current policy is to maintain the current level of immigration to the UK, which is around 300,000 people a year, and to exempt certain sectors – such as the tech and IT industries – from border controls.

Disgraced snooker player Stephen Lee is seeking redemption in China as he looks to help the next generation of players at the snooker academy run by his former mentor, Ding Junhui. Three-time world quarter-finalist Lee, 54, was banned from the sport for life in 2019 after a cheating scandal. He was caught using excessive gift aids and excessive rubbing of the cue on the head string on the cue ball on three separate occasions, a practice which is heavily frowned upon in the sport. The Englishman thought he would never play again, but he has found a new lease of life teaching and mentoring Chinese youngsters in the bustling city of Guangzhou. "I was delighted to be asked to join the snooker academy and I'm thoroughly enjoying it," Lee said in an interview. "The kids here are top class and it's great to be able to give back to the game that gave me so much over the years. "I've always said that teaching is my new career and I feel more fulfilled than I ever did competing in tournaments." China has revolutionised the sport since 2005, producing a wealth of talented players that includes three world champions - Ding Junhui, Bingham and Mark Williams's Chinese roommate in China, Zhou Yuelong. And Lee believes his experience and longevity in the game can help the next generation of Asian stars push the boundaries. "I'm not as intimidating as I used to be, but the kids relate to me anyway," Lee said. "I've been down the same road they are going down now, and I've achieved quite a bit. "For me to say 'I've been there, done that, and got the t-shirt' is not just a phrase, I've actually done it. "It's going to be a big challenge for me, testing me to the limit like I've never been before, but I'm really up for it." Lee claims he is being continually impressed by the youngsters' potential. "The standard of the kids here is incredibly high," Lee said. "There are 14-15 year-old kids that are already beating players who are 25-26 years old, which is amazing. "They need guidance, they need confidence, and they need someone to believe in them. My course is not just to teach them the quickest way to pot a ball, it's to make them understand the importance of discipline, patience and sportsmanship."

In a deeply divided and emotionally charged vote, the House of Representatives in South Carolina has decided to take down the Confederate flag from capitol grounds, bringing an end to a long and tumultuous chapter in the nation's history. The move, sparked by a massacre at an African-American church in Charleston last June, has been a year in the making, with lawmakers and citizens grappling with the nation's complex legacy of slavery and racism. The 90-19 vote in favour of the flag's removal comes after countless hours of debate and numerous failed attempts to find a compromise. The issue has pitted lawmakers and residents in the state against one another, with many invoking the symbol of the Civil War as a painful reminder of the ongoing struggle for racial equality. "I am disappointed, but not surprised, that some of my colleagues continue to cling to this symbol of white supremacy," said Representative Todd Rivers, one of the few Democrats who voted against the measure. "This flag has been a source of pain and division for far too long, and it is long past time for it to be taken down." Supporters of the flag, on the other hand, see the issue as one of states' rights and historic preservation. "This flag represents our heritage and our history, and it should not be erased or destroyed," said Representative Richard Skipper, who voted in favour of keeping the flag. "We should be proud of our past, even if it is complicated and painful at times." The debate over the Confederate flag first erupted following the killing of nine African-American worshippers by a self-proclaimed white supremacist at Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston. The shooter, Dylann Roof, had posted a picture of himself holding the Confederate flag on his Facebook page, fuelling outrage and calls for the symbol to be taken down. In the aftermath of the massacre, Governor Nikki Haley called for the flag to be removed from the statehouse grounds, and a compromise was eventually reached that allowed lawmakers to put the issue to a statewide referendum. However, in a surprise move, Republicans on the state legislative committee denied the ballot question from going to voters, effectively deciding to remove the flag themselves. Now, with the bill signed into law, the Confederate flag will be taken down within 24 hours. The erasure of the symbol will be overseen by the South Carolina Highway Patrol, with the Sons of Confederate Veterans and other groups left reeling by the decision.

In the wake of last month's devastating garment factory collapse in Savar, near Bangladesh capital Dhaka, several of the world's biggest fashion retailers have agreed to join the Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh. The accord, which was initially signed by a handful of retailers, has now gained widespread support and features Hennes & Mauritz, group behind popular high street brands H&M, & Other Stories, Cos and Weekday, as well as Inditex, the Spanish-based owners of Zara and other popular chains. The accord commits companies to conduct independent inspections, issue publicly available reports and sign legally binding agreements to improve building safety in the country's textile industry. The deal comes in response to criticism that Western retailers have historically ignored calls to improve safety standards in Bangladesh's largely unregulated garment industry. The tragedy at the Tazreen Fashion factory on November 24 marks the country's deadliest industrial disaster in history, and has sparked outrage over lax safety measures and poor enforcement in the sector. Bangladesh already had strict laws in place governing working conditions, but these were in short supply across the garment industry, while western brands, including Zara and H&M, have been accused of ignoring warnings of safety issues and ignoring pleas for help from workers. Scottish Government Plans to Introduce "Soft Opt-out" Organ Donation System Face Significant Scrutiny The Scottish Government has published its plans to introduce a "soft opt-out" system for organ donation, a move that has been met with a mixture of praise and criticism from health experts, charities, and politicians. The proposal, which aims to increase organ donation rates and reduce the number of people dying on the waiting list, is expected to be debated in the Scottish Parliament in the coming weeks. Under the proposed system, all adults in Scotland would be assumed to be willing to donate their organs after death, unless they opt out or indicate their objection in advance. The government believes that this approach would simplify the organ donation process, eliminate the need for family consent and reduce the number of families who have to refuse the offer of an organ donation for themselves or their loved ones because of a lack of understanding or cultural sensitivity. Health Secretary Shona Robison said: "Scotland's organ donation rate is one of the lowest in the world and we need to do something about it. The evidence from countries that have already introduced an opt-out system shows that it is a effective way to increase donation rates and save lives. "We believe that a soft opt-out system is the right approach for Scotland because it respects the ability of individuals to make their own decisions about their bodies and can reduce the burden on families who are grieving. It is a complex and difficult issue but we believe that, with the support of the public, we can make it easier for more people to donate and save more lives." However, not everyone shares the government's optimism. Dr. Freshwater, chairman of the British Medical Association's Scotland Board, said: "While the intention behind the proposed system is a welcome one, we have concerns about the implementation and the lack of public understanding about the implications. "We also have concerns about the requirement for a 'soft opt-out' system to be phased in over 18 months, which will put additional pressure on already stretched NHS resources. We will be working closely with the Scottish Government to ensure that any new system is safe, effective and meets the needs of the public." Meanwhile, charity groups such as Kidney Research UK have welcomed the proposal, saying that the current system is too complex and often fails to release donor organs that could save lives.

Mario Testino, one of the world's most celebrated photographers, has long been synonymous with capturing the glamour of A-list celebrities and fashion royalty. His iconic images of Princess Diana, Duchess of Cambridge Kate Middleton, and countless supermodels have helped shape the global beauty agenda for decades. However, behind the lens, Testino has also been an avid art collector, amassing an impressive private collection of works by some of the biggest names in 20th and 21st-century art. A selection of pieces from this collection will be seen in public for the first time in the UK, as part of an exhibition at the Saatchi Gallery in London, which opens in March. Testino, who is of Peruvian descent, says his love affair with the visual arts began when he was a teenager growing up in Lima. "I was surrounded by beautiful architecture, textiles, and ceramics, and I think that's where my appreciation for art began," he explains. "But it wasn't until I arrived in London, and started studying fine art, that I developed a real passion for collecting." Over the years, Testino has amassed an impressive array of works by some of the art world's most influential figures, including Lucian Freud, Pablo Picasso, and David Hockney. Testino's collection is not just about the art itself, but also the stories and memories associated with each piece. He has a particular affinity for works on paper, which he believes offer a unique insight into the artistic process. "When you own a work on paper, you know that it's a sketchbook, a prototype, a piece in development," he explains. "It's a glimpse into the artist's creative process, and it's that sense of intimacy that I find so compelling." The Saatchi Gallery exhibition will feature over 30 works from Testino's collection, including paintings, sculptures, and prints by artists such as Francis Bacon, Jasper Johns, and Elizabeth Peyton. The show promises to be a highlight of the London art calendar, offering audiences a rare glimpse into the private world of this enigmatic photographer and his extraordinary art collection. "I'm thrilled to be able to share my collection with the public for the first time in the UK," Testino says, his excitement palpable.

Jambos boss says he cannot wait to work with the 26-year-old winger who has joined Hearts on a one-year deal from Inverness. New signing Robbie Muirhead has been given a fresh start at Tynecastle after being released by Caley Thistle. "He has a great attitude and is one of the most enthusiastic and hard-working players I've ever met. "He has a real desire to learn and improve his game, which is exactly what I want from a player. "He has already shown that he is a talented player and this is the perfect opportunity for him to get his career back on track. Driver blamed 'blackout' for forgetting horror crash A motorist involved in a devastating head-on collision that claimed the life of five-year-old Dylan Danby, has taken to the witness stand, where he claimed that he cannot recall the moments before, during or after the crash. Sean Baines, 29, appeared in court yesterday to recount the events of April 26, 2018, when his car collided with another on the A1 in North Yorkshire. The impact was so severe that Dylan Danby, who was a passenger in the other vehicle, was pronounced dead at the scene. Baines, who is on trial for causing death by careless driving, claimed that he suffered a blackout due to a previously undiagnosed condition known as autoimmune encephalitis, and therefore has no recollection of the events leading up to the crash or the actual collision. 'I don't remember if I saw the car I collided with or if I applied the brakes,' Baines told the court. 'My next memory is being in a police station, hours later, and being questioned by the police.' The prosecution, however, disputes Baines' claim, arguing that he had ample time to react and avoid the collision, and therefore should be held accountable for the fatal incident. They point to certain inconsistencies in Baines' testimony, including inconsistencies in his alibi and conflicting accounts of the moments leading up to the crash. The jury was also shown footage from Baines' dashboard camera, which appeared to show him driving erratically moments before the collision. The footage has sparked further debate over Baines' account of events. Dylan's family, who have been present throughout the trial, have expressed their outrage at the allegations that Baines is trying to downplay his involvement in the crash. 'How can someone forget a tragedy of this magnitude?' pleaded Jane Danby, Dylan's mother, outside the courtroom. 'It's just incomprehensible.' Baines is being defended by his solicitor, who has argued that his client's bouts of forgetfulness are genuine and are a symptom of his undiagnosed condition. The trial is expected to continue for several more days. The investigation into the crash revealed that Baines had been driving at 66mph in a 60mph zone, and that his car was on the wrong side of the road at the time of the collision. He denies charges of causing death by careless driving and will continue to give evidence next week.

Regulators have given one of the world's largest drug company, Novartis, approval to sell a new gene therapy - a groundbreaking treatment that revolutionises the way diseases are treated at a genetic level. The Swiss pharmaceutical giant's therapy, called Zolgensma, has been cleared to treat a devastating form of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), a rare and orphan disease that causes the loss of nerve cells responsible for controlling voluntary muscle movement. SMA is often referred to as a "death sentence" because it is a degenerative condition that affects babies and young children, resulting in progressive loss of motor function and, ultimately, paralysis and death. Zolgensma - also known as avalglucosidase alfa - works by replacing the faulty gene causing the disease with a healthy one, allowing patients to restore their own muscle function and leading a relatively normal life. The therapy is the first gene-edited treatment for SMA to be approved by regulators anywhere in the world, with the unanimous vote of a panel of scientists at the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Zolgensma will cost more than £1million per dose, making it the most expensive treatment ever approved by regulators. However, the FDA has noted that this is the first disorder in a large class of life-threatening diseases and the approval paves the way for many more gene therapies to come. "We're basically entering a new era of medicine where we can use genetic medicine, and that's exactly what we're doing here," Dr Scott Gottlieb, the FDA commissioner, said. SMA is relatively rare but its treatment represents a massive breakthrough in tackling genetic diseases. Half of those diagnosed with the condition die by the age of two. Zolgensma has shown a dramatic 74% improvement in motor function among patients given the treatment in a clinical trial. Gene editing technology allows scientists to manipulate the genome of the recipient, using various techniques to add, delete or correct genetic code. This breakthrough treatment has long been highly anticipated, with experts saying that it could be a new standard of care for SMA patients. Novartis predicts that more than 1,000 SMA patients will receive Zolgensma in its first year alone, making it a lucrative treatment. While the price of the therapy will undoubtedly place a significant strain on healthcare systems around the world, patient advocates have argued that the benefits of Zolgensma far outweigh the costs. "Offering SMA patients access to Zolgensma is a game-changer," said Terry Heiman-Patterson, chair of the Cure SMA board of directors.

Apple's investors are spooked. The tech sector's largest player has had a dismal few months, with shares falling more than 20% since February's peak and a string of profits warnings that have spooked Wall Street. Analysts have questioned the company's ability to adapt to changing consumer habits and the rise of competitors, while the group's ambitious plans for augmented and virtual reality technology have yet to pay off. Apple has been punished for signs of weakness on a range of fronts, including China, the US and emerging markets, leaving investors wondering whether the once-unstoppable giant is finally starting to lose its mojo. The iPhone - the key to the company's success - has suffered particularly badly, with sales falling 15% in the latest quarter, prompting chief executive Tim Cook to described the situation as a 'soft quarter.' The iPhone X may have set a new benchmark for smartphones, but if consumers are holding off on buying the latest models it could spell trouble for Apple's bottom line. Apple typically derives around 50% of its revenue from the iPhone alone, and so any decline in sales has a disproportionate impact on the company's overall financial performance. But it's not just the iPhones that have been a problem, analysts say. In China, perhaps Apple's biggest growth market, sales have slowed significantly, mainly due to a downturn in demand for the latest iPhone models. The company has also been hit by the US-China trade tensions that have shown no signs of abating, leading to the introduction of tariffs on Chinese imports by the US government. This has knocked Apple shares, which have fallen by almost 10% this month alone. With Apple now expected to report profits of around $11.20 a share for the last quarter - down from a forecast of $13.39 just a few weeks ago - Cook will need to deliver a solid plan to reassure investors that the company still has the firepower to disrupt the tech landscape. But that's not all. Apple's relatively high cost structure - largely a legacy of its acquisition of Beats, the music streaming service, for $3bn - has left some analysts questioning whether the company has the pricing power to navigate the current weak consumer mood. Coupled with the reported struggles of Apple's services business, and the forecast of 30% decline in streaming revenue, a sour mood hangs over the stock, at least among several major investors that remain highly critical of the management's distribution of shares in the last quarter.

England fly-half Toby Flood is on course to miss the start of the Six Nations Championship with a knee injury. The scrum-half, 31, though suffered the injury in training last week and is expected to undergo a scan to determine the full extent of the damage. Ed Slater, the Exeter Chiefs lock, revealed that the injury is thought to be a grade one MCL injury, though further scans will be required to confirm the diagnosis. "I do know that Toby did a training drill last week and felt it a bit, but thought it would be nothing," Slater said. "It's just one of them things that happens in training. "He was rubbing it a bit and didn't go on for the rest of the session, but was hoping it would settle down overnight. When he woke up, it was still sore so they've sent him for a scan. I think it's looking like a grade one MCL." A grade one MCL injury is a strain of the medial collateral ligament, which runs down the middle of the knee, and in most cases it heals without the need for surgery, though the timescale is often a key determinant. With the Six Nations Championship kicking off on the 3rd of February, the risk of missing the opening game against Italy is squarely on the table, although it is thought that Flood can still make a return before the end of the tournament. The European Commission has proposed a new EU Border and Coast Guard agency, as part of a package of measures to tackle the massive influx of migrants arriving in Europe. The proposals, put forward by EU Commissioner for Migration and Home Affairs Dimitris Avramopoulos, would see the creation of a new EU agency, capable of deploying up to 1,000 border guards and coast guards at short notice to support EU member states grappling with migrant numbers. Under the proposal, the agency would allow any EU member state to ask for assistance if it is facing a serious crisis at its borders, such as Greece and Italy have in recent months. Member states could request the deployment of border guards and coast guards, as well as other equipment and resources, such as Frontex ships and planes, to help them deal with the influx of migrants. The plan has been met with a mixed reaction from EU member states, with Southern European countries that have borne the brunt of the migrant crisis so far generally welcoming the proposals. "This is a major step forward in the EU's efforts to strengthen its external borders and ensure the safe and orderly management of migration," said Italian Prime Minister Matteo Renzi. "We need to make sure that those who come to our shores do so under safe and legal conditions, and these proposals would help us to achieve that." Scientists studying the outbreak of Ebola in West Africa have made a chilling discovery: the virus may have adapted to infect human tissues more easily than previously thought. Researchers at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) in the United States have been analyzing genetic data from Ebola samples collected during the 2014-15 outbreak in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. Their findings, published in the journal Science, suggest that the virus underwent significant changes early on in the epidemic, allowing it to infect humans with increased efficiency. At the beginning of the outbreak, Ebola was thought to be spreading slowly, with cases and deaths mounting in a few isolated areas. However, as the epidemic grew, the pace of transmission accelerated rapidly, and the virus began to sweep through West African countries at an alarming rate. It was during this period that the virus underwent a series of genetic mutations, researchers claim. According to the study, the Ebola virus that emerged during the early stages of the outbreak was more primitive and had a higher rate of mutation than the virus that was circulating in later stages. This has led scientists to speculate that the virus may have initially struggled to infect humans, but as it mutated, it became more adept at finding its way into human cells. "This study suggests that the Ebola virus underwent a certain level of adaptation early on in the outbreak, which could have contributed to its rapid spread," said Dr. Anthony Fauci, Director of NIAID, in a statement. "These findings highlight the importance of studying the evolution of infectious diseases and understanding how they adapt to new environments." The researchers also found that the virus underwent changes in its genetic material, known as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), which allowed it to bind more effectively to human cells. This increased binding capability may have given the virus an advantage in terms of transmission, allowing it to jump from host to host with greater ease. While the study sheds new light on the Ebola virus's rapid adaptation to infect humans, it also underscores the need for continued research into the virus's behavior and the development of effective treatments and vaccines. "The Ebola virus is a formidable opponent, and its ability to adapt quickly to new environments is a key factor in its ability to cause outbreaks," said Dr. Sarah Pett, a member of the research team.

Libya's Struggle for Stability: Five Years On Five years after the Arab Spring protests swept Libya, toppling the 42-year regime of Muammar Gaddafi, the North African nation remains mired in chaos and instability. The revolution that began on February 15, 2011, and ultimately led to the dictator's death on October 20 of that year, was meant to bring about a new era of freedom and prosperity to Libya. But instead, the country has been plagued by continuous conflict, infighting between rival factions, and a crippling lack of governance. In the intervening years, multiple attempts at forming a unified government have fallen short, and Libya is now effectively divided into three main regions: the internationally-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA), which controls the western coastal cities, including the capital, Tripoli; the rival Libyan National Army (LNA), led by General Khalifa Haftar, which dominates eastern Libya; and the Islamic State (IS) militants, who have carved out a territory in the southern desert. The inexcusable situation has left Libya without a single government with authority over the whole country, and it is civilians who pay the heaviest price. A staggering 400,000 people have been displaced since the conflict began, with millions more left without access to basic necessities like healthcare, education, and electricity. The humanitarian crisis in Libya has been exacerbated by the constant turmoil. Last year, medicine, medical equipment, and other essential supplies were blocked from entering the country for over 50 days due to a blockade imposed by the rival forces. Meanwhile, Libya was forced to rely on foreign aid to meet the critical needs of its population, with reports indicatiing that hundreds have succumbed to treatable illnesses and diseases due to the lack of access to medical care. Regional and international organizations have been meeting in an attempt to resolve the crisis, but the numerous peace talks and negotiations have failed to deliver a lasting solution. On the contrary, the increased tensions between the opposing forces in recent months have brought the country to the brink of civil war. The failure to establish a stable government has cost the country dearly. According to the World Bank, Libya's economic output has shrunk by over 60% since 2014, eradicating decades of development efforts. With no stable government to collect taxes, Libya has virtually no taxation system, making it one of the most lucrative havens for smuggling, corruption, and organized crime in the region.

Baby Vaccination Breakthrough Ground-breaking new research has hailed a vital step forward in the fight against a devastating illness that affects thousands of babies every year. Scientists at the NHS's Centre for Immunisation Research and Surveillance have announced that early human trials of a new vaccine to protect against Group B Strep (GBS) have shown spectacular promise. group b strep gift illustration Families across the country will welcome the exciting news, as the potentially deadly illness claims the lives of a handful of babies every week. GBS is a bacterial infection that can cause life-threatening complications in newborn infants, with the greatest risk to babies born prematurely or at low birthweight. According to figures released by the NHS, GBS is estimated to kill 320 babies a year in the UK, and another 750 suffer from lasting disabilities. The problem is compounded by the fact that GBS accounts for around 20% of all stillbirths, and can cause often severe and disabling conditions such as meningitis, pneumonia and sepsis, which affects babies more than a week old. Researchers in Cambridge and Bristol, who co-led the trial, declared the breakthrough discovery at the European Congress of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases in Amsterdam, as they revealed the impressive results from 72 volunteers who took part in the study. He explained that while the results outlined these positive outcomes and although there have been no concerning adverse effects reported during the trial, the antibody profiles produced in the studied babies will now require assessment to confirm a measurable response before the ability of the vaccine can be confirmed to effectively prevent the transmission of the GBS bacteria. This vaccine trial finally moving towards an eagerly anticipated second phase testing trial looking to expand the participant caseload consists of elderly individuals over 60 and infants born with weakened immune systems. Ministers and Health officials have welcomed the breakthrough, expressing optimism that it might one day offer the prospect of protecting newborn babies from this serious illness. But it's a long road ahead for the new vaccine, and regulatory approval will only come after rigorous further trials involving thousands of mothers-to-be and their babies. Mrs Joy Greensmith, Chair of Group B Strep Support, the leading charity fighting the group, hailed the trial as a major breakthrough.

Foreigners Investing in Australian Property: Breaches of the Law a Major Concern The Australian government has revealed that around 40 foreign nationals have been identified as possibly breaching the country's residential real estate investment laws. This development has raised concerns among lawmakers and regulators, who are working to ensure that Australia's property market remains open to legitimate foreign investment while remaining protected from malicious activities. According to the government, the alleged breaches include individuals who have acquired property in Australia without meeting the necessary requirements, such as being granted an Australian business number, holding a tax file number, or disclosing details of their financial situation. Some individuals are believed to have also failed to comply with the disclosure requirements under the Foreign Acquisitions Takeovers Act, which demands that all foreign entities or individuals notify the Treasurer when making investments in Australian property. The revelations come after the government intensified its efforts to monitor foreign investment in Australian property, following concerns that some foreigners have taken advantage of the country's relaxed rules to buy up residential homes and rent them out at inflated prices. The government has also been under pressure to address the growing discrepancy between the high demand for housing, particularly in Sydney and Melbourne, and the shortage of affordable homes for ordinary Australians. Australian Treasurer, Josh Frydenberg, has signaled that the government will be taking a tougher stance on compliance with the foreign investment laws, stating: "We are working closely with regulatory agencies, such as the Australian Taxation Office and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), to ensure that foreign investors comply with Australia's laws and regulations." While the government did not reveal the names of the individuals or the countries they are from, experts believe that the problem of foreign nationals exploiting loopholes in the system is widespread. The real estate market watchdog, Choice, estimates that up to 20% of Australian real estate listings are occupied by foreigners, including Chinese, Indian, and Middle Eastern investors. Industry insiders fear that unless the government takes action to address these issues, Australia's property market may become increasingly accessible to those who are not genuine investors but rather seen as unwanted speculators. "For too long, there has been a lack of integrity in our property market," stated Choice's CEO, Alan Olsen. "It is imperative that we hold these individuals accountable to ensure that ordinary Australians have access to a level playing field when buying and renting properties."

Microsoft will have a significant say in Nook Media's business strategy going forward and will work to build out the division's streaming services to both the US and international market.

Black African, Black Caribbean, and mixed-heritage pupils also outperformed their white British counterparts in both maths and reading. The notion that success at the very pinnacle of sport is a direct result of someone's unrelenting dedication and unyielding work ethic is a premise that is often and loudly espoused. Throughout the world of elite athletics, you will find coaches, pundits and sportswriters alike repeatedly haranguing the next crop of young talent, urging them to put in that extra hour at the gym, to run just one more kilometre on the treadmill, to do just one more set of burpees after their workout. Plain cigarette packaging could lead to a significant reduction in smoking rates in the UK, according to a major review. The review, published in the journal Tobacco Control, suggests that eliminating brand logos and other advertising from packaging could lead to a reduction of 300,000 smokers in the next year. The study, which was conducted by a team of researchers from the University of Stirling and the University of Sydney, used data from Australia and New Zealand, where plain packaging was introduced in 2012 and 2016, respectively. In these countries, the study found that smoking rates among people aged 45 and under plummeted. Australia's smoking rate fell by 0.8 percentage points among people under 45, while New Zealand's smoking rate decreased by 1.4 percentage points among the same age group. The researchers estimate that these changes would translate to a reduction of around 300,000 smokers in the UK, assuming the same results are seen. Plain packaging is a policy that has been advocated for by health experts for many years, who argue that it helps to reduce the attractiveness of cigarettes and make them less appealing, particularly to young people. Smoking remains one of the leading causes of preventable death in the UK, with around 78,000 deaths per year attributed to smoking. Tobacco companies have vigorously opposed plain packaging, arguing that it breaches their trademark rights and could lead to smuggling. However, the UK government has stated its intention to introduce plain packaging in the near future, and the findings of this study may add further momentum to that decision. Dr. Gerry Stimson, a senior research fellow at the University of Stirling and one of the authors of the study, said: "Our results suggest that plain packaging can have a significant impact on reducing smoking rates among young people, which is a population that is hardest to reach with anti-smoking messages." He added: "We believe that the evidence is now clear that plain packaging can be an effective tool in reducing smoking rates and that the UK government should move forward with implementing this policy." However, some opponents of plain packaging have expressed concerns that the policy could lead to an increase in the illicit trade of tobacco products, which could offset any public health benefits. The tobacco industry has also argued that alternative methods, such as increased taxation and public education campaigns, could be more effective in reducing smoking rates.

Emotional Freedom: The Surprising Key to Happiness For a long time, researchers have sought to uncover the secret to happiness. We've heard that gratitude is key, that mindfulness is essential, and that setting achievable goals is a recipe for success. But a recent study has shed new light on the factors that contribute to our overall well-being, and the findings may surprise you. According to the research, published in the journal Emotion, people are happier when they are able to feel the emotions they desire - even if those emotions are unpleasant. Anger, hatred, and even fear are not necessarily barriers to happiness, but rather indicators that our emotional lives are rich and fulfilling. The study, which involved over 350 participants, asked participants to reflect on the emotions they experienced in their daily lives. The researchers then analyzed the responses to identify patterns and correlations between emotions and happiness. What they found was fascinating: people who reported feeling a wide range of emotions - including negative ones like anger and frustration - were more likely to report being happy and fulfilled than those who only experienced positive emotions like joy and contentment. But why? According to Dr. Jennifer Weston, the lead researcher, the key to happiness lies in the concept of emotional freedom. "When we're able to feel our emotions in the moment, we're more likely to experience a sense of freedom and autonomy," she explained. "This allows us to live more authentically and genuinely, which is essential for happiness." The study also found that the intensity of the emotions didn't matter - it was the ability to feel them that was most important. "It's not about whether we're feeling happy or sad, but rather whether we're able to feel our emotions at all," said Dr. Weston. So, what does this mean for our daily lives? Rather than striving for a constant state of euphoria or happiness, perhaps we should focus on allowing ourselves to feel whatever emotions arise - even the uncomfortable ones. This might mean taking time to reflect on our emotions, practicing mindfulness to stay present, or simply being tolerant of our own feelings. Of course, this isn't to say that wallowing in negative emotions is the solution. But rather than suppressing or denying our feelings, we need to learn to acknowledge and accept them as a natural part of the human experience. As the researchers conclude, "The pursuit of happiness may not be about achieving a particular state, but rather about embracing the complexity and diversity of human emotion."

Liberal Democrat Schools Minister David Laws has reiterated his party's pledge to increase teachers' pay to a level where they feel valued for their hard work in the classroom. Speaking at the Left-bank Forum in central London, Mr Laws said: "I'm a great believer in teachers' pay being a way to show people that they are valued in their job. And I think that's something that the Lib Dems want to do more of." The Lib Dem leader Nick Clegg announced earlier this month that his party would increase pay for new recruits to the profession by 20% over the first five years of their career, if they win the general election next year. "We want to recruit more teachers to the profession," Mr Laws explained. "And we want to make sure that they come to this job with the expectation that they will be valued and paid properly for it. We think that the proposed increase in pay for new recruits will attract more talented individuals to become teachers." The Liberal Democrats are keen to stress that their plan is not aimed at middle-aged teachers, but rather at young and ambitious newly qualified teachers who are desperate to enter the profession. Mr Laws said: "If you believe, as I do, that the best teachers are going to be the ones who are most passionate and most talented and most certain of their own abilities, then you've got to value those qualities. And you do that through their pay packet." Currently, new teachers in England only start on around £22,000 a year. Their salary increases as quickly as possible over the next 10-15 years, but the Lib Dems' proposals would speed up this process. "We've got to get to a situation where being a teacher is a job that's highly regarded and respected by the public," said Mr Laws. "It's going to be a big challenge for any political party who wants to promise the earth to the teaching profession. But I think we can make a good case that we value teachers through their pay packet and give them a pay rise that shows we value their commitment to the job." For some experienced teachers, however, the Lib Dem proposals might seem a bit piecemeal. Christine Hodgson, a maths teacher at Patcham High School in Brighton, expressed concern that the government was failing to address the long-standing pay inequalities that exist in the profession.

The 14th Conference of the Parties of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) has brought together representatives from over 180 countries to discuss and agree on measures to protect threatened species. The conference, which is being held in Johannesburg from 24 November to 5 December, is the largest single gathering of global governments and stakeholders dedicated to the conservation of wildlife and the regulation of international trade in endangered species. At the heart of the conference is the bitter debate over the survival of elephants. The demand for ivory has led to the slaughter of tens of thousands of elephants each year, and conservationists are calling for stricter measures to prevent the trade. However, some African governments are pushing for a relaxation of the rules, arguing that it would allow them to reap the benefits of the ivory trade and boost their economies. South Africa, which hosts the conference, has been criticized for its stance on the ivory trade. In 2017, the country ended a 24-year ban on ivory sales, sparking outrage among conservationists. The decision was seen as a blow to efforts to protect elephants, which are listed as vulnerable to extinction by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). "This conference is a crucial opportunity for governments to come together and agree on measures to protect species, including elephants," said Dr. Jane Smart, Head of IUCN's Global Protected Areas Programme. "The ivory trade is a major threat to elephant populations, and we urge all countries to take a firm stance against it." The conference is also expected to discuss the future of rhinoceros conservation. The poaching of rhinos for their horns continues to be a major problem, with over 1,000 killed last year in South Africa alone. Conservationists are calling for tougher measures to stop the trade and protect these iconic animals. Delegates at the conference will also discuss the impact of climate change on species conservation. Rising temperatures and changing weather patterns are expected to have a major impact on biodiversity, and the conference will consider ways to mitigate the effects of climate change on species. In addition to the debates on elephants and rhinos, the conference will also consider measures to protect other threatened species, including lions, leopards, and pangolins. The conference is expected to agree on a list of species to be protected, as well as measures to regulate international trade in endangered wildlife.

One of the most significant discoveries comes from the Ngandong site, where archaeologists uncovered a range of tools crafted from stone and wood. Analysis of these artifacts suggests that the primates of group G were highly skilled hunters, utilizing various techniques to catch their prey, including ambushing and running down their quarry. But these primates weren't just clever hunters; they also demonstrated a sophisticated understanding of their environment. Excavations have revealed evidence of controlled fire use, further cementing their status as among the most intelligent and resourceful non-human primates of all time. Primate archaeology has also shed light on the complex social dynamics of our ancient cousins. At the Ngandong site, researchers have found remains of clan members aged from neonates to elderly individuals, suggesting a thriving family unit with social hierarchies and cooperative hunting strategies. In one remarkable excavation, scientists discovered a set of 354 stone tools arranged in a specific pattern, sparking debate among researchers about whether this represents an example of primitive language or perhaps even the earliest form of art. The significance of this discovery, if confirmed, would be akin to uncovering the very first grandfather clock and gaining insight into the minds of our distant ancestors. Dr. Madelene Lukas, a leading primatologist and expert in primate archaeology, enthuses about the groundbreaking findings emerging from this field. "By excavating the past of our primate cousins, we're gaining a deeper appreciation for the evolution of intelligence, creativity, and innovation - traits that are fundamental to our own species."

Scott Gregory is no stranger to the world of golf. The 23-year-old from Nottingham is making his professional debut at the US Masters, one of the most prestigious and historic tournaments in the game, where some of the world's greatest golfers have tested their skills for decades. Despite being just 10 months into his professional career, Gregory has made a major impression on the golfing world, winning the Asian Tour's Gujarat Co-operative Bank Open in January. The young golfer's impressive game has already caught the attention of golfing legends, and now he's setting his sights on the green jacket that's the ultimate goal for any golfer who participates in the Masters. However, as Gregory begins his new chapter in one of the game's most gruelling tournaments, he knows that no amount of practice or strategy will be enough to guarantee success. That's why he's turned to YouTube for some expert advice, hoping to find in the wealth of information available online the perfect formula for a successful debut. "I've been watching more videos than I ever have before in preparation for the Masters," said Gregory in an interview, explaining that watching veteran pros like Jordan Spieth, Rory McIlroy and Adam Scott has given him valuable insight into their pre-shot rituals and course study. Scott Walker's dreams of the presidency have finally come to an end, as the Wisconsin Governor announced his decision to withdraw from the Republican nomination race. After months of struggling to gain traction, Walker's campaign has become increasingly unsustainable, weighed down by dwindling contributions and plummeting poll numbers. Despite his initial promise as a front-runner, Walker's bid for the White House has suffered a series of setbacks, leaving him with no choice but to bow out. Walker's campaign, which was once seen as a serious contender, had been struggling to find its footing since the summer. Despite his efforts to reconnect with voters and reinvigorate his message, the Governor's poll numbers continued to slide, never quite regaining the momentum he had initially experienced. As the days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, it became increasingly clear that Walker's chances of becoming the Republican nominee were rapidly evaporating. The final nail in the coffin came in the form of lackluster fundraising numbers, with Walker's campaign reporting a paltry $6 million in quarterly contributions, a far cry from the $13 million he had boasted of just a few months prior. With his campaign coffers woefully depleted, Walker was left with little choice but to throw in the towel, avoiding a potentially embarrassing defeat in the Iowa caucuses. Walker's decision to end his campaign is a significant blow to his supporters, many of whom had invested great hope in his bid for the presidency. As a staunch conservative, Walker had endeared himself to many in the Republican base, and his withdrawal will likely create a vacuum that will be eagerly filled by other aspirants. In a statement announcing his withdrawal, Walker expressed his gratitude to his supporters and pledged to continue fighting for the principles he believes in. "While there was a clear desire to defeat President Obama and turn the page on his failed policies, it has become clear that I do not have the same momentum going into the Iowa caucuses and beyond," Walker said. "I want to try a different path, and throw my support to a different candidate." As Walker exits the fray, the Republican field will likely undergo significant shake-ups, with various contenders vying to fill the void left by the Wisconsin Governor.

Tragedy Struck the Hajj Pilgrimage In one of the deadliest incidents to strike the Hajj pilgrimage in years, a massive construction crane collapsed in the Muslim holy city of Mecca on Friday afternoon, sending tons of twisted metal and concrete crashing to the ground. At least 107 people have been confirmed killed in the disaster, with many more injured and still recovering in hospitals. The site of the tragedy is the Masaa pedestrian underpass near the Grand Mosque in Mecca, a location previously deemed safe and renovated just a few years ago. The area was crowded with thousands of pilgrims, many of whom had gathered for evening prayers when the crane suddenly gave way. The Saudi government has swiftly announced an investigation into the cause of the crane collapse, vowing to uncover the root of the disaster and prevent similar incidents in the future. Interior Minister Prince Mohammed bin Nayef Al Saud briefed the country on the tragedy and the efforts underway to assist the victims and their families. In a statement, he said, "The King and I have ordered an immediate investigation in this incident... We are doing our best to help the victims and their families." Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the deputy crown prince and defense minister, has also pledged a thorough inquiry into the collapse, which would include experts and officials from the interior, foreign, and Hajj and Umrah ministries. Witnesses have described the moments leading up to the tragedy as chaotic and heart-wrenching. Many pilgrims had gathered in the underpass while waiting for evening prayers to begin, although some have reported hearing a loud crash before falling debris began to rain down. "There was a loud noise, like a bomb exploding," one eyewitness told the BBC. "People started screaming, and then there was dust and smoke everywhere." Abdul Karim Abu Julma, a pilgrim from Egypt, told Reuters that he saw the crane fall but did not see any flames or explosions. "It just came crashing down," he said. The pilgrim arrived in Mecca for the Hajj on September 10 and was at the queue for prayers when the incident occurred. "I was praying with my eyes closed. There was a shout, I opened my eyes, and I saw the crane on top of us. I was covered in dust and couldn't breathe. My friend was screaming and shouting nearby." The pilgrim received several shallow wounds that have left him with a concussion.

Jamil Daniels, a 31-year-old former officer with the Milwaukee Police Department, was charged on Tuesday with first-degree reckless homicide in connection with the shooting of Joel Acevedo on August 7. Acevedo, a 29-year-old man, was shot multiple times while being held down by Daniels in Milwaukee's Riverwest neighborhood. According to the criminal complaint, Acevedo was shot after being beaten and restrained on the floor by Daniels and at least one other officer. A lengthy investigation by the Milwaukee County District Attorney's Office found that Acevedo died from a combination of blunt force trauma and multiple gunshot wounds. Officials say that the shooting was not justified and that Acevedo was already subdued at the time he was fired upon. Documents obtained by the local media show that the investigation found that Acevedo was sprayed with pepper spray while being restrained, and that Daniels then punched him in the face, causing him to fall to the ground. Despite being in a prone position and handcuffed, Acevedo was shot twice by Daniels. "When I looked up and saw my brother on the ground, I thought to myself, that couldn't be," Moses Acevedo, Joel's brother, said at a press conference after the charges were announced. "It's like my world came crashing down around me." The shooting sparked outraged protests in Milwaukee, with many community members calling for greater accountability within the police department. The Milwaukee Police Department has faced intense scrutiny in recent years over issues of police brutality and racial profiling. In 2016, then-Officer Dominique Heaggan was acquitted in the shooting death of Dontre Hamilton, a 31-year-old man who was being detained when he was fired upon by Heaggan. In 2020, Officer Joseph Mensah was fired from his position after his involvement in the shooting of three men over a two-year period, including the shooting of Jay Anderson Jr. in 2016. Daniels has been suspended from the police department pending the outcome of the case. The Milwaukee Police Department said it "takes these types of allegations very seriously" and will co-operate with the District Attorney's Office as they continue to investigate the shooting. If convicted, Daniels faces up to 60 years in prison. "Our office is committed to ensuring that public officials and law enforcement are held to the highest standards of integrity and accountability," said Milwaukee County District Attorney John Chisholm in a statement on Tuesday.

The Royal Air Force is facing a crisis of numbers, with a catastrophic decline in the number of fighter jets on standby to defend British skies, defence experts have warned. According to a report by think-tank Royal United Services Institute, the number of multi-role Typhoons is set to fall to just 24 by 2025, a decrease of over 70% on the 87 aircraft that were operational just six years ago. This decline is happening at the same time as increased threats from Russia, China and other aggressor nations, fueling fears about Britain's ability to defend itself effectively. "We are sleepwalking into a disaster," said a senior defence official who asked not to be named. "The number of Typhoons we have is going to be the lowest in the history of the RAF. We are an island nation surrounded by powerful enemies and our air capability is being allowed to erode at an alarming rate." The report, which studied ministry of defence data, found that the number of frontline Typhoons has been steadily declining since 2011, in part due to the decline of military aviation budgets, but also because of the ongoing delays and problems with the F-35 Lightning II stealth fighter, which is due to arrive in the RAF in the next few years. These delays mean that the RAF will not receive the planned cohort of fresh F-35s to upgrade its air power, which could lead to a further decline in the overall number of operational aircraft. "If the trends we have seen over the past few years continue, then by 2025 we will have just three squadrons of Typhoons, each consisting of just 8 aircraft," said Paul Beaver, an aviation consultant. "This will be almost equivalent to standing up a blank wall and calling it a front line capability." The decline in RAF numbers has been confirmed by senior military sources who point out that the Typhoon fleet will have to take on a heavier burden of operational responsibilities, with ongoing commitments in Afghanistan and the Middle East, as well as the prospect of new missions against Russian-backed forces in Eastern Europe. The ministry of defence has pushed back on the idea that a significant reduction in Typhoon numbers will leave Britain's air power weakened, saying that the jets will remain "invincible" in battle and that the real danger to Britain's security is "not the bloody £2 billion plane", but rather the broader issues around European defence co-operation and Russian aggression.

Coroner's probe into Martin Place cafe siege opened Two years after the devastating hostage crisis in Martin Place, a coroner's inquest has finally opened into the events that unfolded on that fateful day in December 2014. On Thursday, Coroner Michael Barnes began hearing from witnesses and examining the circumstances surrounding the siege at the Lindt cafe, in which gift wrapping manager Man Haron Monis, an Iranian-born self-styled cleric, held hostages hostage for 16 hours before police stormed the building and shot him dead. The siege ended in tragic circumstances, with Monis killed and two hostages, Katrina Dawson, 38, and Tori Johnson, 34, dying as a result of gunshot wounds suffered during the final moments of the stand-off. Speaking at Sydney's Coroners Court on Thursday, Mr Barnes paid tribute to Dawson and Johnson, saying their families deserved answers to the questions surrounding the events of December 15 and 16, 2014. Mr Barnes explained that the inquest would examine the circumstances of the siege, including the actions of NSW Police and the protocols they followed during the crisis, as well as the role of the New South Wales government and its agencies in responding to the siege. He noted that the inquest would also investigate Monis's psychology, his extremist ideology and his links to terrorism, which have been revealed through intelligence gathered since his death. The inquest is likely to hear evidence from hundreds of witnesses, including hostages, police officers, and experts in the fields of psychology and counter-terrorism. New South Wales Police have confirmed that some of its senior officers, including Commissioner Andrew Scipione, will appear before the inquest. While there has been intense scrutiny of the police response to the siege, Assistant Commissioner Mark Murdoch defended the actions of his officers, saying they had acted in a "reasonable and proportionate" manner to end the stand-off. Mr Murdoch also acknowledged that the coroner's inquest would provide a critical examination of the crisis and the subsequent investigation. The inquest will resume again on 7 February. The families of those killed in the siege say they are relieved that the inquest has finally begun and are hoping for the truth about the events surrounding their loved ones' deaths to be revealed. "We're looking forward to hearing the evidence that will be presented at the inquest," said James Packer, Dawson's brother-in-law.

The long and bitter dispute over guard procedures on Southern Railway trains came to an end yesterday when train drivers, represented by the ASLEF union, agreed to call off their series of strikes which have severely disrupted commuters and caused widespread anger from passengers. The deal, which is subject to ratification by ASLEF members, strikes a balance between the group's demands for improved staffing and the company's push to move towards driver-only operation of its trains. Under the agreement, a "minimum safe staffing regime" will be implemented on certain Southern services, thereby preserving the role of train guards. This will also lead to the reinstatement of jobs that had been cut as part of the company's efforts to mothball certain train carriages.
