India has launched its first air quality index, to provide real time information about pollution levels. People can now check the air quality in their city or region on a mobile app or website, which gives them an instant picture of pollution levels, impact on their health and what they can do to reduce their exposure. The air quality index is a crucial tool to combat the nation's worsening air pollution, which is caused by the burning of fossil fuels, inadequate waste management, and industrial emissions. India has eight of the world's 20 most polluted cities, according to a World Health Organization report last year. Long-term exposure to polluted air has serious health implications, including lung diseases, heart problems, and even premature death. The new air quality index will categorise pollution levels into six colour-coded categories, ranging from 'Good' (AQI 0-50) to 'Hazardous' (AQI over 300), with corresponding advice on mitigating exposure. For example, for 'Good' air quality, weekly activities outdoors should be fine, while for 'Hazardous' conditions, people are advised to stay indoors, avoid strenuous activities and perform critical tasks like firefighting. Minister of Environment, Forest, and Climate Change, Prakash Javadekar, said that the government is taking all necessary steps to improve air quality in our cities as well as industrial areas. "Our industrial units and vehicles will be monitored regularly. Even residents can monitor their personal air quality by fitting an air quality monitor at their home. It's part of our effort to monitor and improve air quality." The index was launched by the Ministry of Environment, in collaboration with several state governments and leading air quality measurement agencies. It will provide updates on real-time basis across 51 cities and 598 air quality monitoring stations across India. In addition, an open-source microgrids initiative has been initiated to help authorities to monitor the air quality in cities with reduced contamination. Online bulletin boards have been made to check and compare the efficiency of different cities for reducing air pollution. By assessing pollution levels and categorizing areas as "Good", "Moderate", "Poor", "Very Poor", and "Severe", authorities will be well-equipped to respond to crisis situations and develop measures to control and eradicate sources of pollution. Awareness among citizens will be increased through the released smartphone applications regarding air quality monitoring. With several major cities that remain highly contaminated with PM 2.5 including Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chandigarh, and Kolkata, this can prove to be a crucial life-saving initiative.

His warning is based on projections from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), an expert body that advises governments on the science of climate change. The UK's Chief Medical Officers (CMOs) are to publish new guidelines on safe drinking limits after a 20-year review. The guidelines, which are due to be published on Thursday, have been updated to reflect new evidence on the impact of drinking on health. Members of the public are being warned that the current guidelines of 14 units per week for men and 14 units per week for women could be reduced, and that the benefits of drinking in terms of social occasions and relaxation should not be used as an excuse to ignore the risks. The review has been led by Professor Sir Ian Gilmore, a Liverpool University professor and former president of the Royal College of Physicians. He has said that the current guidance is "out of date" and that the review will take into account "developments in science and new evidence". "The CMOs regularly review the evidence on various health topics and the guidance on alcohol is one of the most often asked for," Professor Gilmore said. "We have looked at all the evidence and we're now ready to issue new advice on how much is safe to drink." The updated guidelines, which will cover the whole of the UK, will take into account relevant research from the UK and internationally, including studies on the risk of certain cancers, heart disease, and liver disease. The review will also look at different types of drinking, including binge drinking and heavy drinking over a long period of time. According to Public Health England, excessive drinking costs the NHS £3.5 billion a year and is associated with over 4,000 deaths. In addition, drinking problems are a major cause of stress on relationships, social problems and domestic violence. Last year a study found that alcohol-related hospital admissions had increased by 33% over the past decade and that one in five drinkers in the UK is either an "every-day drinker" or binge drinker. The British Heart Foundation welcomes the review, saying that it is crucial that the public is made aware of the risks of excessive drinking. "We know that the current guidelines are not being followed by many people, particularly among those who drink more than 14 units a week," a spokesperson said. "It's crucial that the public is made aware of the risks associated with excessive drinking and how it can affect their health." The government said that no decisions had been made regarding the new guidelines, which will be revealed after the publication of the review on Thursday.

Jez Green, a highly respected coach known for his work with top English clubs, says his first impressions of the England women's team before the World Cup were "shocked" and that he quickly got to work on overhauling the team's fitness approach. Green's experience with the squad shortly before the 2015 tournament has been widely reported, but in an interview he has given fresh insight into just how radically he revamped the team's coaching methods. The former Blackburn Rovers and Coventry City coach, who has also worked with World Cup winning teams such as England's Under-17 and Under-20 teams, and English club Newcastle United, joined the England squad less than a month before the World Cup, where they reached the semi-finals. He explained how, as soon as he joined, he established what he believes is a "simple and effective" approach that "gets the facts on performance and can predict the outcome" of matches, rather than relying on "theories" of how players perform. Since joining, Green has overseen significant improvements in the team's results and physical fitness levels and although there have been instances of injuries, the trend was, and remains, an upward one. "We progressed from getting absolutely belted around by world-class teams to playing world-class teams almost at the same level, and if we'd have had another four or five months in, God knows what I think we would have done." Green revealed how the changes the team implemented under his guidance helped "build that confidence" among the players and that there's been a lasting shift in the squads approach. Iraqi forces launched a long-awaited assault on the Old City, the last stronghold of so-called Islamic State in Mosul, on Sunday, but their advance was met with fierce resistance from ISIS fighters. Troops from the Iraqi army's Counter-Terrorism Forces, backed by US-led coalition air strikes and artillery fire, began pushing into the ancient neighbourhood, once home to over 150,000 people. However, the militants have rigged the streets and buildings with explosives and launched a barrage of gunfire and mortar bombs as the troops tried to make headway. The first day of the operation saw clashes between Iraqi forces and Isis fighters trapped in the narrow, densely populated streets of the Old City. "Progress is being made," said Major General Sami al-Aridi, who is commanding the Counter-Terrorism Forces, on Sunday evening. "We are advancing and the operation is going according to plan." But if that sounds reassuring, the reality is that it's proved an extremely bloody day with soldiers on both sides suffering heavy casualties. One Iraqi officer who asked not to be named told Reuters that dozens of soldiers had been killed or wounded in the fighting. The officer added that Isis fighters had also dug tunnels and basements, which made them almost impossible to target. The Old City is a maze of narrow alleyways and closely packed buildings, with residents forced to become human shields as Isis fighters have taken up positions among the civilians. It's been two years since Isis, also known as Daesh, captured Mosul, and while Iraqi forces have been gaining ground for months, the recapture of the city remains an uphill battle. In recent weeks, Isis has significantly increased its use of booby traps and improvised explosive devices, which have caused severe setbacks for the Iraqi military. As the Iraqi forces move deeper into the city, they will be aware that the Old City remains one of Isis's most fortified strongholds, and the battle will only intensify. "Daesh has deployed large numbers of fighters from all over the world, including China, Chechnya and Syria," Major General Qasim Atmos, the Iraqi military's operations commander, warned before the attack. In a nod to the strength of its resolve, Isis has posted several online statements denying that the Old City had even been captured. But local residents told Reuters that Isis fighters have become increasingly panicked in recent days, having taken cover in shallow graves that they dug in the region's soil.

Charity groups that help the homeless, vulnerable children, and animal welfare rely on donations to fund their life-changing work. But in an effort to boost fundraising, they are increasingly buying data lists of householders to send personalised, "cold" letters. The practice, known as "direct mail", is common in the charity sector but has raised concerns about its effectiveness and use of donor data. Some groups claim that the letters can generate significant income, while others have rejected the practice saying it is intrusive or ineffective. An investigation by the BBC's Panorama programme has uncovered a series of charities that use data brokers to buy lists of householders. These lists, often sold by recruitment agencies or data companies, can be based on everything from electoral roll data to online shopping habits. Charities may then use this information to tailor their appeals, highlighting causes that are most likely to resonate with the recipient. For example, if a data list shows a family has previously donated to an animal welfare charity, a direct mail appeal for a similar charity may be more successful. Penny Luker, director general of the Institute of Fundraising, admits that the charity sector does use data lists. She says, however, that it is "ultimately a heavy heart decision" for many charities as there is "a psychology to charity fundraising and the idea of setting off with a blank sheet can be daunting". Some high profile charities that have used direct mail campaigns include Oxfam, the RSPCA, and the British Red Cross. Between them, these charities have spent millions on letter-shots in the past few years. In 2018, the RSPCA used data broker, hoist, to send tailored appeals to over 800,000 households, generating almost £1.5 million in donations. But not all charities are keen on the practice, with some questioning whether it is an invasion of privacy. "It's just the elderly being bombarded with beg letters," says Hilary Yelland, from pensioner group, Age UK. "Everyone should be treated equally. No one should be given preference over someone else just because they have given to another cause." Age UK itself is against direct mail and reluctantly accepts cash only donations. The Mail Preference Service (MPS) and the Fundraising Preference Service enable individuals to suppress their data from being sold to this purpose. Charities say they adhere to data protection policies but there is a growing trend that solicits data in various manners on social media, at high street retailers or at charities retailers.

The Indian-owned firm has put the site at the centre of a review into its UK operations, sparked by falling demand and high energy costs. "Port Talbot steel works is not just a valuable industrial asset, but also a vital element of the industrial heritage of Wales," he said. Tesco Mobile has launched a new ad-funded content service called AdGo, which will allow customers to download music and movies at discounted prices, as well as access exclusive content and deals, in return for watching adverts on their mobile phones. The idea is that customers can cut their monthly mobile bill by as much as £5 a month, as well as enjoying other perks and rewards. According to the company, AdGo will enable customers to choose from a range of music, film and TV shows, including popular titles such as The X Factor, Britain's Got Talent, and demand TV series such as Peep Show and The IT Crowd. They will also be able to access exclusive content, such as behind-the-scenes footage, interviews with celebrities, and other premium content, without having to pay extra for it. But there's a catch - customers will have to watch a set of three-minute adverts every week in order to get the discounted prices. They can choose when to watch these adverts, with most content available for weekly, monthly or per session access. AdGo is similar in concept to the existing ad-funded services such as Sky's On Demand offer. The Tesco Mobile service is described as giving customers complete control over the adverts they see and how often they watch them. Tom Maltes, Managing Director, Tesco Mobile, said: "AdGo is a unique offer that lets our customers choose the moments when they watch our adverts and access a huge range of content and exclusive deals for free, or at a discounted rate. "This is part of our long term plans to revolutionise the mobile industry and bring customers more choice, more control and more value for money. Our aim is to continually surprise and delight our customers by making their Tesco Mobile experience more enjoyable, and by doing that, more rewarding." Tesco Mobile is the third biggest mobile network operator in the UK. This new low-cost offer consists of bespoke content purchases that let customers buy exclusive offers and downloads with an option to pay via a highly competitive pay-per-view model or to access content, again for the first time, via a smartphone app. Experts say that the effectiveness of ad-funded content is still up for debate, and its success will depend on how well customers find the service. They will have to see whether they are offered enough to make watching adverts more tolerable.

Finland is consistently ranked among the top-performing countries in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) league table, alongside countries such as Singapore and Hong Kong. The country's schools have a reputation for being some of the most relaxed and least stressful in the world, yet they still produce students who consistently achieve better grades than those from many countries with more rigid and demanding education systems. So, what is the secret behind Finland's success? One of the main differences between the Finnish education system and those in other countries is the amount of time spent in school. Finnish students spend around 1,100 hours in the classroom each year, compared to 1,300 hours in the UK and US. This is one of the lowest numbers in the OECD and is significantly lower than the recommended number of hours by the National Education Association (NEA). But despite the shorter school day, Finnish students typically do less homework than their international counterparts. A survey by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) found that Finnish 15-year-olds reported doing an average of one hour and 13 minutes of homework each night, compared to 2.5 hours in the UK and 2 hours in the US. Finland's approach to education is underpinned by a set of core principles that are designed to help children become curious, self-directed and lifelong learners. The curriculum is designed to be flexible and adaptable, with a focus on developing critical thinking skills, creativity, and problem-solving abilities. Children are encouraged to explore and investigate topics through play and hands-on learning, rather than simply following a traditional textbook-based approach. One of the most distinctive features of the Finnish education system is the emphasis placed on teacher training and professional development. Finnish teachers are typically drawn from the top 10% of graduates and undergo a rigorous two-year training programme, including a period of classroom-based training and a dissertation. This focus on teacher quality is reflected in the fact that Finnish teachers consistently rank among the highest in terms of professional excellence, according to the OECD. Finland's commitment to early childhood education is also worth noting. The country has a comprehensive system of childcare and pre-school education, which includes universal childcare for all children from birth to 5 years old. This has been shown to have a profoundly positive impact on children's educational outcomes, both in the short and long term.

Alcohol's threat to a healthy lifestyle is well documented, with studies consistently showing that excessive drinking can lead to a range of health problems, from liver disease to heart conditions. But new research suggests that regular heavy drinking may also increase the risk of skin cancer, one of the most common types of cancer worldwide. Scientists have discovered that drinking too much alcohol can trigger a series of chemical reactions in the body that ultimately make the skin more susceptible to the damaging effects of UV radiation. The study, published in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology, involved researchers from Johns Hopkins University in the United States. They conducted experiments on mice to see how the introduction of ethanol - the type of alcohol found in beer, wine, and spirits - into their systems affected their skin and DNA. What they found was striking: the mice that had been exposed to ethanol showed significant changes in the DNA of their skin cells, leading to the formation of abnormal and precancerous cells. This suggests that repeated bouts of heavy drinking may weaken the skin's natural defences against cancer-causing mutations, making it more likely that skin cancers will develop. "What we found is that the ethanol in alcohol can induce an increase in the production of reactive oxygen species," said Dr Stephen Gluckman, one of the study's lead researchers. "These are unstable molecules that damage our DNA, and can lead to cancer. When we exposed the mice to UV radiation, the recipients of ethanol showed a higher rate of skin damage and mutations than the controls." Dr Gluckman's team also found that although the damage caused by ethanol-induced oxidative stress could be reversed by removing the DNA damage repair pathways in the skin cells, this did not fully eliminate the cancer risk. The study's findings have significant implications for public health and our understanding of the risks associated with heavy drinking. They suggest that people who enjoy a regular tipple may need to be more mindful of the damage their lifestyle could be doing to their skin and overall health. As Dr Gluckman put it, "these findings highlight the potential link between heavy drinking and skin cancer, and suggest that people who consume excessive amounts of alcohol may be more susceptible to skin damage and cancer." With an estimated 132,000 cases of skin cancer diagnosed each year in the UK alone, the potential risk posed by heavy drinking demands more research and awareness-raising.

Thai Army Officer Warrantued Over Rohingya Trafficking A Thai court has issued an arrest warrant for a senior army officer accused of being involved in the trafficking of Rohingya migrants from Myanmar and Bangladesh. Major General Manas Kanetsuk, a high-ranking official in Thailand's 41st Ranger Battalion, is allegedly linked to a human trafficking ring that smuggled thousands of Rohingya across the country, putting many of them at risk of being sold into slavery. The move comes as a significant blow to Thailand's military government, which has come under increasing pressure from human rights groups and international critics over its handling of the Rohingya crisis. Amnesty International has called for the Thai government to take immediate action to prevent the further exploitation of Rohingya migrants. Major General Manas, 62, who has commanded troops in Thailand's far south province, denies any wrongdoing and says the allegations are a personal vendetta against him by his rivals within the military. However, in a sign of the seriousness with which the case is being taken, Thailand's army chief has ordered an investigation into the charges. Court document seen by the international media show Major General Manas, who is currently at large, is accused of collaborating with human trafficking ringleaders, including a former politician and a well-known tycoon in Tom Yum Goong, a certain seaweed dish. The ringleaders were arrested in 2015 and have since confessed to trafficking around 15,000 Rohingya migrants from Myanmar and Bangladesh. The Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority, have faced intense persecution in Myanmar, sparking a massive refugee crisis that saw hundreds of thousands flee to other countries in the region. Many Rohingya have been trafficked across the border to Malaysia and Thailand, where they are often forced into prostitution, forced labor, and other forms of exploitation. Thai authorities maintained last year that Rohingya people were not trafficked in Thailand. Officials claimed that they had "absorbed the elderly, women and children into a support centre and provided medical care and ongoing settlement arrangements." The support centre though, collapsed in 2019, deporting numerous Rohingya migrants back into the conflicts-ridden region. A string of accidents on the packed boats have killed scores, adding to an alleged collective remembering impression for traffickers often staying thousands of miles from Thailand. The International Organization of Migration says thousands of Rohingya have been trafficked this year alone. Many are at risk of being sold into slavery.

In an age of digital disruption and fragmentation of content, the question of what constitutes the most important source of news and the most powerful media organisation in the world today is more complex than ever. However, one name keeps rising to the surface: The New York Times. Founded in 1851, The New York Times, commonly known as "The Times," has long been regarded as one of the most authoritative and respected publications in the world. Its influence extends far beyond its New York-based circulation and is felt globally, with a presence in over 160 countries and a multilingual online edition that is available to readers in many different languages. The paper's investigative journalism and in-depth reporting on a wide range of topics, from politics and business to culture and science, has earned it a reputation for excellence and has often set the agenda for media coverage around the world. In fact, a study by the leading media analysis company, PolitiFact, found that 96 per cent of all American newspapers and TV stations rely on The Times for at least some of their reporting, while in Britain, the paper has often been at the centre of mainstream media discourse. The influence of The Times is such that many of its high-profile scoops have driven news narratives globally, attracting attention from celebrities, politicians, business leaders and ordinary readers. One only needs to look at some of the most impactful news stories of the past few years to see the New York Times' remarkable reach and impact. In 2013, its revelations about Edward Snowden's NSA Leaks shook the world, generating a global debate about data privacy and government surveillance, and was even nominated for a Pulitzer Prize. In 2015, it exposed the massive tax avoidance scheme by Apple, that almost doubled its tax rate in the US and forced Ireland to consider changing tax laws. Today, with well over 6 million subscribers to its online edition, The New York Times is regarded by many as the gold standard of journalism. According to the Pew Research Centre's annual excellence in journalism report, in 2019, the paper landed the top spots in eight different category awards, including 'Investigative reporting', 'Beat reporting' and 'Breaking news photography'. Critics have long pointed out that The New York Times is an elite voice that often fails to interact with or understand 'regular people' and this charge has become more vocal lately.

Glen Travis Campbell, a man with a voice as smooth as honey and a legacy that spanned multiple decades, left an indelible mark on the music world. Born on April 22, 1936, in Billstown, Arkansas, Campbell's rise to fame was nothing short of remarkable, and his contributions to country music are still celebrated today. With a career that spanned over five decades, Campbell's path to stardom was not without its challenges. A self-taught musician, Campbell learned to play the guitar at the age of four and was heavily influenced by the sounds of gospel and Western Swing. After serving in the United States Army, Campbell moved to Albuquerque, New Mexico, where he formed his own band, The Western Wranglers. It was during this period that Campbell began to hone his craft, taking on various musical projects and performing across the American Southwest. Campbell's big break came in the 1960s when he joined the Gerald Fried Orchestra, a popular weekly television show featuring country music. This exposure eventually led to a recording contract with Capitol Records, and in 1962, Campbell released his debut album, 'Big Giant Slumber Party,' which included his first hit single, 'Rockin' Robin.' However, it was his appearance on the Andy Williams Show, where he performed a duet with Michelle Phillips, that catapulted Campbell to stardom. The exposure led to further collaborations with other popular artists, cementing his status as a first-rate vocalist. Campbell's crowning achievement came in 1967 with the release of 'Gentle on My Mind,' a song he co-wrote for the film 'True Grit,' which won the Academy Award for Best Original Song. However, it was the following year that Campbell truly achieved stardom, both nationally and internationally, with the release of his cover of Rudy the Raindrop's 'Wichita Lineman.' This melodic masterpiece showcased Campbell's incredible vocal range and heartfelt delivery, solidifying his position as one of the premier country singer-songwriters of his generation. Campbell's romantic and often poignant ballads contributed to a record number of marriages and divorces within his fan base. Love songs like 'Galveston' and 'Loving Her Was Easier (Than Anything I'll Ever Do Again)' tap into the heartache and longing that defined Campbell's songs. In addition to his country hits, Campbell delved into other genres, showcasing his wide range and musical versatility. Collaborations with the Everly Brothers and Keith Gigan, rock legend Madcat Ruth, saw him dare to explore areas beyond the realm of country and Americana genres.

Two riders were hospitalised on Sunday after separate crashes during the RideLondon-Surrey 100, a 100-mile amateur cycle event that takes participants though some of the most scenic roads in Surrey and London. The accident marred an otherwise successful event, which saw tens of thousands of cyclists from around the world come together to tackle the iconic route. The crashes occurred on different parts of the course, with one rider suffering a serious injury on the infamous Box Hill section, a notorious climb near Dorking. An MTW ambulance service spokesperson confirmed that a 59-year-old man was taken to St George's Hospital at Tooting with multiple injuries, including fractures. "We attended the scene at around 12.30 pm after reports of a cyclist being injured and took the man to hospital for treatment," the spokesperson said. The man was said to be in a stable condition and his injuries were not thought to be life-threatening. In the second incident, a 42-year-old man lost control of his bike on a descent near Reigate and collided with a verge before coming to a stop. He was treated by paramedics on the scene before being taken to a London hospital for observation. A statement from the London Ambulance Service said: "We were called at 1.40 pm to reports of a cyclist having a medical emergency. "We sent a bike ambulance crew, two ambulance crews, and an incident response officer to the scene. "We treated a 42-year-old man at the scene before taking him to St Thomas' Hospital by ambulance for further care." A spokesperson for the event said safety was always the top priority and that riders were reminded to follow the rules of the road and to report any incidents to the authorities. "As with any large-scale event, unfortunately, there were some incidents which were unavoidable," the spokesperson said. "We are grateful that the riders involved are currently receiving the care they need and will continue to do everything in our power to ensure the safety of all participants and spectators at our events." The RideLondon-Surrey 100 has been plagued by problems in the past, including a grandfather who died after being involved in a crash on the course in 2016. The event has since introduced a number of safety measures to try and mitigate the risk of accidents, including the use of 'pile course marshals' to help divert riders at areas which are difficult to negotiate.

A highly-respected and experienced Scotland Yard commander involved in a major police operation which ended in tragedy is being allowed to retire, it can be revealed. The move has sparked outrage among police watchdogs and Labour MPs who claim that justice has not been served. The Metropolitan Police's head of professional standards recommended the senior officer, a Superintendent, for promotion despite him being under investigation over the fatal shooting of a man by armed police. James Dipple-Johnstone, of the Met's professional standards department, described the officer in a report as "outstanding" and added that his "integrity and professionalism" appeared to be "chipper" - a key requirement for promotion. However, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is currently investigating the operation, which left father-of-one Coco McCabe dying of a gunshot wound in Croydon. The incident, which marks the fifth fatal shooting by the Met in the past year, has raised questions over the threshold for the use of lethal force. Mr McCabe, 38, died after a hypothetical "art attack in progress" led to armed officers surrounding his car, before one of them opened fire. In a statement, the Met said: "It is the individual's decision whether to continue serving as an officer, having considered their future and career development. The decision was taken in line with Met policies and procedures." The Met have said that the investigation is ongoing and the report dealing with Superintendent's career, and his eligibility for promotion, is being withheld until it is complete. The inquiry into the circumstances surrounding Mr McCabe's death is continuing but Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Bernard Hogan-Howe has said that the use of force by the officers was "proportionate" and "justified". Despite this view, Labour's policing spokesperson, Jack Dromey, MP, expressed his dissatisfaction with the decision to let the officer retire. "It's frankly outrageous that an officer who is at the centre of an ongoing investigation is being allowed to pension off and retire. It smacks of double justice and undermines trust in the police," he said. "The public needs to know why such an individual was allowed to continue serving as an officer and why they've been cleared for promotion." The Metropolitan Police's Commissioner, Sir Bernard Hogan Howe, said that the decision was part of routine course and this this "highly experienced and dedicated officer" will be dealt with by the courts if the IOPC's investigation leads to any charges.

The eternal debate surrounding tennis and the Olympics continues to cause a stir among fans and pundits alike. While some might argue that the sport's elite professionals would be better off focusing on their lucrative careers rather than donning the coveted Olympic rings, the overwhelming consensus among the sport's top players is clear: they want to compete in the Games. Novak Djokovic, one of the most successful players of the current era, has been a vocal advocate for Olympic participation. He has spoken at length about the significance of the Olympics and the pride that comes with representing his country. And he is not alone. Rafael Nadal, the Spanish superstar, has also been an enthusiastic supporter of the Olympics, often referencing the honor of wearing his nation's colors and competing alongside the world's best. Serena Williams, one of the most dominant female players of all time, has echoed similar sentiments. She has spoken about the unique opportunity the Olympics presents: "It's not just about winning a tournament; it's about representing your country, being a part of history, and making a statement on the world's biggest stage." These sentiments are reflected in the impressive turnout at the Olympic Games. Year after year, the world's top tennis players flock to the various Olympic venues, eager to don their national colors and compete for the coveted medals. And yet, despite the enthusiasm of the players, there remains a lingering question about the suitability of tennis in the Olympics. Proponents of the sport's inclusion argue that it provides a platform for the world's greatest players to compete in a unique and electric atmosphere. Detractors, on the other hand, point to the fact that tennis is a professional sport with its own lucrative tour, and that participating in the Olympics can often come at a significant cost to the players. This criticism is not without merit. Many players have spoken about thegrueling schedule they maintain during the Olympic years, often missing out on valuable Grand Slam preparation time in order to compete in the Games. And there's the small matter of prize money – or the lack thereof. While the Olympics do offer a modest financial reward to its competitors, it pales in comparison to the millions of dollars that players can earn on the professional circuit. And yet, despite these challenges, the allure of the Olympics remains undiminished.

Charity Calls for Expansion of Fertility Treatment for Scotland's Couples As Scotland continues to be at the forefront of groundbreaking medical research, one charity is pushing for greater access to fertility treatment for couples struggling to conceive. The Christian charity, OneBodyOneFaith, is urging the Scottish Government to extend the funding for IVF (In Vitro Fertilization) from two to three cycles, citing the distress that multiple failed attempts can cause for couples. The charity is highlighting the fact that couples in Scotland can currently receive funding for up to two cycles of IVF if they meet certain criteria. While this is seen by many as a generous provision, many couples go on to have multiple cycles, further straining finances and placing a significant emotional burden on families. OneBodyOneFaith is urging the Scottish Government to expand the funding to include a third cycle of IVF, arguing that this would go some way in alleviating the financial stress often faced by couples during this time. In a statement, the charity said, "Fertility treatment is a costly and time-consuming process, and the stress of repeated failure can take a significant toll on couples. An additional cycle of IVF would be a lifeline for those who have already faced disappointment." Researchers have found that multiple failed attempts at IVF can actually reduce the chances of success, as well as increase anxiety and depression in couples. OneBodyOneFaith is drawing attention to this reality, warning that couples may be forced to make distressing decisions about the number of cycles they can afford, adding to the emotional pain already felt during this intense period. Dr Sharon Corscadden, a lecturer in social sciences at the University of Stirling, has also weighed in on the issue, commenting, "Couples who are struggling to conceive often face unseen but real costs, including lost earnings, mental stress and emotional toll. Larger life plans like family development, buying a house, or friends and family expectations may be impacted. Extra funding for further cycles of IVF could make a real difference in people's lives, enabling them to keep their dreams within reach." The Scottish Government has come under increasing pressure to address the unique challenges faced by couples in the country, particularly those struggling with fertility issues. It now remains to be seen whether OneBodyOneFaith's campaign will yield tangible results, and whether this £20,000 lifeline will give hope and a greater sense of security to Scotland's most vulnerable couples.

The world of sport and beyond is mourning the loss of a true legend as boxing great Muhammad Ali passed away on Friday at the age of 74. The three-time heavyweight world champion and humanitarian left an indelible mark on the sport and beyond during a lifetime of unparalleled success and countless charitable endeavours. Charity groups and homelessness campaigners have expressed alarm at the findings, warning that the data undermines efforts to address homelessness. Under anti-social behaviour laws, people can be arrested and fined for begging in England and Wales if they refuse to leave an area. Last year, 57 out of 2,681 (or 2.1%) people arrested for begging in England and Wales were classed as homeless by police, according to data obtained by BBC Breakfast through Freedom of Information requests. The figures show that 50% of those arrested for begging were from London, where a borough-by-borough analysis reveals that in the worst-affected areas, fewer than 1 in every 10 people arrested for begging were homeless. In one London borough, Havering, the proportion of homeless beggars was as low as 0.4%. The findings come at a time when homelessness is rising, with official statistics showing that on any given night, more than 4,700 people in England are sleeping rough. Marshajane Thompson, 59, is a former rough sleeper who now works with the homeless. "These figures are sick, to be honest with you," she said. "They show how out of touch the authorities are with the reality of homelessness." The arrest and prosecution of beggars has been widely questioned by charities, including the Salvation Army, which argues that the approach fails to address the root causes of homelessness. "We don't believe that arresting people, prosecuting them, and imposing fines is an effective solution to the issue of begging," said the Salvation Army's Trevor Prier. London Mayor Sadiq Khan was also critical of the approach. "The data raises serious questions about the effectiveness of these measures and the need for a more holistic and understanding approach to addressing homelessness and rough sleeping," he said. The advocacy group, Crisis, called for measures to tackle homelessness to be prioritised over the policing of begging. "It is beggars who are at risk of being arrested and prosecuted," said the group's Vicky Sorrell. "We need to turn the policy on its head. Instead of concentrating on criminalising and punishing people on the streets, we should be focusing on providing them with the support they need to get off the streets." The Metropolitan Police and the British Transport Police, which are both responsible for policing a significant number of begging arrests, argued that their enforcement policies were aimed at reducing the profile and visibility of street soliciting.

The windswept hills and rugged coastline of County Donegal had become a familiar backdrop for some of my most memorable encounters with Martin McGuinness. As a respected leader and a symbol of peace in Northern Ireland, he had always been a compelling figure, but it was his humility and humanity that left a lasting impression. Last April, I had the privilege of joining him on a walk around an ancient Irish hill fort on the Inishowen peninsula in Donegal. The air was biting, with a chill that cut through even the thickest of coats, but McGuinness, dressed in his usual smart casual attire, seemed completely unfazed. His Labrador, Digby, trotted faithfully by his side, tail wagging enthusiastically as we made our way along the windswept path. As we climbed the hill, the hill fort's ancient stone walls rose up to meet us, their weathered stones bearing testament to the countless generations of Irish history that had unfolded beneath them. McGuinness's eyes sparkled as he shared stories of the fort's rich heritage, his voice carrying above the wind as he spoke of the ancient Celts who had once called this spot home. With each step, he seemed to grow more at ease, his passion for the land and its people evident in every word. As we reached the crest of the hill, the Atlantic Ocean stretched out before us, a vast expanse of grey water that seemed to meet the sky at a distant horizon. The wind buffeted us from the north, threatening to whip our hair into a frenzy, but McGuinness merely wrapped his coat around him, a reassuring smile on his face. "Digby, stay close," he called out to his loyal companion, who obeyed with a wag of his tail. As we stood there, taking in the breathtaking view, I couldn't help but wonder what lay beneath McGuinness's tranquil exterior. A man of such immense influence and complexity, who had walked the tightrope of politics and peace-making for so long, must surely have known his share of turmoil. Yet as we walked, he spoke of nothing but the simple joys of life: the beauty of the Irish countryside, the companionship of his dog, and the importance of taking time to appreciate the world around him. As we made our way back down the hill, the wind died down, and the sun broke through the clouds, casting a warm glow over the landscape.

A team of researchers at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics has made a major breakthrough in the search for life beyond Earth. Using advanced spectrographic techniques, they have detected an atmosphere surrounding the exoplanet K2-18b, a world that has long been of interest to scientists due to its similarities to our own planet. Located about 111 light-years from the Sun in the constellation Leo, K2-18b is one of the most promising exoplanets discovered to date. With a mass that is roughly eight times that of Earth's, it is considered a "super-Earth", meaning that it is larger than our own planet, but not so massive that it would be a gas giant. Announced yesterday at a press conference in the United States, the discovery is the result of a comprehensive analysis of data collected by the Hubble Space Telescope. Using a technique known as transit spectroscopy, the researchers were able to detect the subtle changes in the light passing through the exoplanet's atmosphere as it orbited its star. "This is a major milestone in the search for life beyond Earth," said Dr. Brendan Bowler, the lead author of the study. "For the first time, we have detected an atmosphere around an Earth-like exoplanet, and it's a pretty exciting result." The detected atmosphere is thought to be composed mainly of hydrogen and helium, with potentially smaller amounts of heavier elements such as water vapor and methane. While the presence of such gases does not necessarily imply the existence of life, it does provide valuable clues about the planet's formation and evolution. "We're really interested in understanding the conditions on K2-18b because it could potentially be a world with liquid water on its surface," said Dr. Bowler. "Liquid water is essential for life as we know it, so finding it on another planet would be a game-changer." The discovery of an atmosphere around K2-18b is just the latest in a series of recent breakthroughs in the search for exoplanets and the conditions necessary for life. With the aid of future missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope, scientists are expected to continue making new discoveries that will shed light on the mysteries of the universe. While the road to finding life beyond Earth remains long and challenging, the detection of an atmosphere around K2-18b is an important step in the right direction.

Ambulance staff in England and Wales are facing a "nightmare" of abuse from patients and their families. Figures show that nearly 20% of calls to ambulance control rooms are deemed abusive. Paramedic’s Union, Unison, is calling for tougher penalties to be introduced. Labour MP Steve McCabe, who chairs the parliamentary committee that oversees the group, agrees that gift cards and apologies are not enough to tackle the problem. 'Abuse is endemic in our system.' But many of these incidents never result in a police investigation or a prosecution. Unison is now pushing for tougher sentencing guidelines for those who abuse the service, similar to those for harassment and assault. Paramedic Francesca Mackenzie is leading the campaign. She recalls countless times of being subjected to abuse while doing her job. 'I have been sworn at, insulted, told I am stupid, a waste of space and worse, by the very people who are supposed to be grateful that we are trying to help them.' She said. "It's hard to imagine what is going on in the mind of someone who is so desperate to be seen and heard that they lash out in such a way." Michelle Plush, another paramedic, has been attacked while working for the London Ambulance Service. Her client, who was mentally ill, became aggressive and assaulted her during a call. Despite the ordeal, she says the abuse she receives on the job remains an issue even outside working hours. "People say things like: 'Why didn't you help me sooner?' 'You're incompetent.' 'You don't care about people.' They don't care about the impact their words can have on someone who is just trying to do the best they can." She said. Roger Harding, a policy analyst for the charity Mind, highlights the relatively lenient sentences being handed down to people who abuse the service, despite the severe impact their actions can have on staff. He believes more needs to be done within the community to reduce the prevalence of abuse against NHS staff, including free training on crisis communication and compassion to patients and family. He stresses the vital role NHS staff play 'in a moment of crisis where the public are at their most vulnerable'.

Cameroon's dreams of a strong run at this year's Africa Cup of Nations have been dampened by a more pressing concern for the country's football governing body: the welfare of its local players. The nation has been plagued by a lack of transparency and accountability in contract negotiations, with many players left in the dark over their financial situations. According to Augustin Ngeme, the head of the Cameroon Players' Union, two-thirds of Cameroon's top players do not have a copy of their own contract. This issue is not simply a matter of documentation; it highlights a deeper issue of exploitation and power imbalance in the world of Cameroonian football. "We have been demanding from the start that the Cameroonian Football Federation (FECAFOOT) and the clubs meet certain basic demands in terms of the contracts, things like having copies of the contracts for the players, but despite repeated meetings, the situation has not improved," Ngeme told the BBC. "This is a critical issue and it has been one of our key concerns over the past few years." Cameroon has a rich football heritage, and is one of Africa's most successful nations at the senior level. But Ngeme believes that this success has often come at the cost of the welfare of its players. "It's a story we've been repeating for years now, but unfortunately, it seems that the clubs and FECAFOOT are not taking the necessary steps to protect the players," he said. As a result, many Cameroon players have been left vulnerable to exploitation and abuse. "Sometimes, a player will sign a contract but when he gets paid, he realises that the amount is less than they were promised," Ngeme said. "Other times, players are not paid at all. It's a difficult situation for us as a union, but we are doing everything in our power to support our members." The issue of contract transparency is just one of several concerns facing Cameroonian football. The country has struggled to produce a professional league, and many top players have been forced to seek their fortunes abroad. Despite this, Ngeme remains optimistic about the future of football in Cameroon. "We believe that football can be a powerful tool for positive change in our country," he said. "We are working hard to build a stronger, more responsible football industry that prioritises the welfare of our players."

The Dark Secret of Child Marriage Deep in the heart of a rural village lies a reality that is both devastating and disturbing - that of child marriage. For 17-year-old Agnes, her life took a drastic turn three months ago, when she was married to a man she had never met. The union was arranged by her family, in a bid to secure their economic and social status. But the consequences of this decision have been catastrophic for Agnes, who is a child herself. In a world where poverty and lack of education are rampant, many families believe that marrying off their daughters early is the best way to secure their financial future. The logic behind this lie is simple - a daughter is no longer an economic burden, and her dowry is the key to her family's prosperity. But what about the girl's dreams, aspirations, and most importantly, her human rights? Agnes's story is a stark reminder of the absurdity of child marriage. "I was never consulted about the marriage," she says, her voice trembling with emotion. "I was told that it was my parents' decision, and that I had to do as they said. I was never asked what I wanted or if I was ready for marriage." The trauma and fear in her eyes are palpable, and serve as a stark reminder of the devastating consequences of child marriage. Child marriage is a widespread problem that has been around for centuries. The United Nations estimates that over 15 million girls under the age of 18 are married every year, and nearly 250 million have been married before the age of 15. The consequences of child marriage are far-reaching and devastating - from high school dropout rates, to increased risk of domestic violence, early pregnancy, and maternal mortality. But the statistics and facts only tell a small part of the story. For Agnes and countless others like her, child marriage is a brutal reality that strips them of their childhood, their agency, and their human dignity. "I want to go back to school," Agnes says, her eyes filled with longing. "I want to have friends, to learn, and to have a career. But now, I'm married and tied down to a man who doesn't even know me." The battle against child marriage is a fight for the rights of girls like Agnes. It is a fight against ignorance, poverty, and inequality.

The devastating fire that engulfed the Grenfell Tower apartment building in west London has sparked widespread outrage and sadness. The tragic loss of life, which now stands at 30 confirmed dead with many more presumed dead, has been met with shock and dismay from the public and politicians alike. However, as the full extent of the disaster becomes clearer, it has become increasingly apparent that the government has ignored crucial lessons from previous tower block fires. The 24-storey tower block, a social housing building in the Latimer Road area of Kensington, was completed in 1974 and was home to over 600 people. The fire, which started in the early hours of Wednesday morning, spread rapidly through the building, trapping many residents inside. The cause of the fire is still unknown, but it is clear that a combination of factors, including the cladding and insulation used on the building's exterior, have contributed to the blaze's severity and spread. A similar cladding system was used on another London tower block, Lakanal House in Camberwell, which had a major fire in 2009. The investigation into that blaze, which killed six people, warned that some building insulation materials may not be safe for use on high-rise buildings. In fact, the department allowed similar cladding materials to be installed on another West London tower block, the Chalcots Estate, which had a partial fire last year. Speaking in Parliament, Communities Secretary Sajid Javid acknowledged that the cladding material was a contributing factor in the Grenfell Tower fire. Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn called it a "manufacturing scandal" and has called for a full inquiry into how buildings like Grenfell were allowed to be constructed without adequate safety standards. "This isn't just a Grenfell problem, it's a London problem, it's a Britain problem," he said. "How many times do we need warnings and disasters to make a change? The latest generation of Virtual Reality (VR) technology has been a game-changer, revolutionising the way we interact with and experience digital content. From immersive gaming experiences to cutting-edge medical applications, the possibilities offered by VR are endless. One of the most significant innovations is the development of high-resolution, high-field-of-view VR headsets. Equipped with advanced graphics processing units and sophisticated tracking systems, these headsets enable users to engage in fully immersive virtual environments like never before. The precursor to modern VR technology was the helmet-mounted display, first demonstrated by Ivan Sutherland in the 1960s. However, it wasn't until the introduction of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1990s that VR started to gain traction. The first consumer-grade VR headset, the Virtual Boy, was released by Nintendo in 1995. Though it failed to gain significant popularity, the trend had been ignited, and subsequent innovations have transformed the industry. In recent years, the emergence of Oculus Rift, Vive, and PlayStation VR has propelled VR to the mainstream. These cutting-edge headsets provide users with an unparalleled level of immersion, rendering the boundaries between reality and fantasy increasingly blurred. The possibilities for entertainment, education, and even therapy are vast. Gaming companies such as Unity, Epic Games, and Valve have all thrown their weight behind VR, creating a wealth of interactive content that's pushing the limits of what we thought was possible. Beyond the realm of entertainment, VR has numerous practical applications. In medicine, VR is being used to simulate surgical procedures, allowing surgeons to hone their skills in a realistic, risk-free environment. Additionally, VR therapy is being used to treat a range of mental health conditions, from PTSD to anxiety disorders. The potential for VR in education is equally vast, with immersive educational experiences allowing students to explore historical events, microorganisms, and other topics in a way that's engaging, interactive, and unforgettable. In a related development, the rise of augmented reality (AR) technology is facilitating a seamless blend between virtual and physical spaces. Devices such as the HoloLens and iPhone 12 Pro come equipped with AR capabilities, transforming the way we navigate, interact, and engage with digital content. The proliferation of these devices signals an exciting new frontier in human-computer interaction and encourages us to rethink the course of this technology. Thanks to the rapid advancement of VR technology, a greater number of people are now participating in the VR ecosystem than ever before.

In a study published in the journal Science, researchers revealed that the spots on a leopard's coat act as a form of "psychoactive camouflage" that fool the brain into perceiving the animal as a "not a circle" - essentially rendering the leopard invisible in the grasslands it inhabits. This is because, in the leopard's habitat, animals with fewer spots or those in a vertical orientation are more likely to blend into the background, making it easier for them to stalk their prey. Similarly, the stripes of a tiger act as a form of "attention-grabber" in the dense forests it roams. Researchers suggest that the stripes serve as a high-contrast visual signal that warns potential predators to stay away, thereby offering the tiger a vital survival advantage. But how exactly do these markings work? According to researchers, it's not just about aesthetics. By observing the way light interacts with the markings, scientists can determine the "carnivore-weighted visual scene", which is the critical component of the big cat's camouflage strategy. This concept implies that the spots and stripes work by suppressing certain wavelengths of light that are characteristic of the forest environment, thereby preventing predators from detecting the big cats. By manipulating the visual sensory perceptions of potential predators, the big cats are able to stay one step ahead of their adversaries. These findings have profound implications not only for our understanding of animal camouflage but also for wildlife conservation efforts.

In a BBC radio interview, Mr Mitchell said he had been a "scapegoat" for the police's failure to recover his lost bike. He claimed that he was unfairly pilloried by the media and the police over a row that sparked widespread outrage and calls for his head from the Opposition. India's emergence as a global economic powerhouse is a phenomenon that has left even the most seasoned economists and investors in awe. The reasons for this rapid growth are numerous, and gift-edious credit is due to the visionary leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who has implemented a series of policies designed to stimulate economic growth and attract foreign investment. One of the key drivers of India's economic miracle has been the development of its vast IT industry. From a humble starting point of just a handful of companies a few decades ago, India has become the world's leading outsourcing destination, with many multinational corporations outsourcing their software development and other business processes to Indian companies. The likes of Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro, have become household names not just in India but across the globe, and have spawned a plethora of smaller entrepreneurs and start-ups who are now beginning to make a mark in their own right. The country is poised to become the world's third largest consumer market by 2030, and boasts a demographic dividend, with over 65% of its population under the age of 35. A massive sixgill shark, measuring over 15ft in length and estimated to weigh more than 1.3 tonnes, has been caught off the coast of County Clare, Ireland. The enormous creature, described by local fishermen as a "monster", was hauled out of the Atlantic Ocean by the crew of a fishing boat, the "Convoy Knoll". The shark, which was caught on a lure and weighed on board, is believed to be the largest sixgill shark ever recorded in European waters. According to eyewitnesses, the shark was swimming in shallow water around 1.5 miles off the coast of Doonbeg in County Clare. "We've been fishing these waters for years, but I've never seen anything as big as this," said captain James O'Riordan of the "Convoy Knoll", a fishing boat based in Kilrush. "It took us over an hour to reel it in, and the fight was intense. The men on board were exhausted by the time we finally landed it." The sixgill shark (Hexanchus griseus) is a rare and deep-sea dwelling shark that can be found in all the world's oceans. It is characterised by its six gill slits, a flat, broad head, and a distinctive megalodon-like appearance. While not typically as large as tiger sharks or great whites, the sixgill shark can reach impressive sizes, with reports of individuals reaching up to 20ft in length. Scientifically speaking, the shark caught off County Clare is believed to be a juvenile or sub-adult sixgill, as mature individuals of the species do not typically reach the same size. According to Dr Paula Keogh, a marine biologist at the University of Galway, "Sixgill sharks like this one are highly valued in scientific research, as they provide insights into the feeding habits, migration patterns, and ecological niche of these deep-sea predators." While the shark was safely brought on board the fishing boat, it was not brought ashore for examination. Capt. O'Riordan said, "We let it go soon after we landed it, as we didn't want to harm it further. We just wanted to see this incredible creature and know that it's out there, living in our waters." The massive shark was tracked back into the ocean, several miles from the point of capture. News of the incredible catch has sparked both excitement and concern among local residents and fishermen. "Sharks this size can have a significant impact on local marine ecosystems, as they are apex predators and critical components of our ocean's food chain," said Kieran O'Keeffe, a marine conservationist who has been working to protect the marine environment off County Clare.

The European Union has faced criticism for its handling of the migrant crisis, with many accusing policymakers of failing to provide adequate support and resources to deal with the influx of migrants. With no end in sight to the tide of migrants, policymakers must navigate a delicate balance between maintaining border security and respecting the fundamental rights of those seeking refuge.

£60m Tagging System Fails to Deliver as Predicted Five years ago, the Ministry of Justice unveiled a pioneering plan to introduce a state-of-the-art GPS tagging system to track offenders on bail or parole. However, a damning report has revealed that the system has not only failed to meet its deadlines but has also failed to provide any tangible benefits. The report, produced by the Ministry of Justice's own inspectors, paints a stark picture of a scheme that has been woefully mismanaged and under-resourced. The Telecare system, which was supposed to be rolled out to 10,000 offenders within two years, has yet to be fully implemented. To date, only a handful of pilots have taken place, and the results have been underwhelming. A key selling point of the system was that it would allow authorities to monitor offenders in real-time, flagging up potential hotspots and enabling swift intervention. However, the inspectors found that the system's performance is often hampered by poor connectivity and frequent outages. Furthermore, the report highlights significant concerns about the data generated by the system. With offenders often breaching certain areas or deliberately tampering with their tags, authorities are struggling to distinguish between genuine attempts to abscond and technical malfunctions. As a result, only a small proportion of offenders are being successfully tracked, leaving many vulnerable communities concerned about public safety. The £60m investment has also raised concerns about value for money. With only a fraction of the expected number of offenders being monitored, the cost per user is ballooning. At a time when budgets are being squeezed and pressure is mounting to reduce reoffending rates, the Telecare system's lacklustre performance is bound to raise eyebrows. The report's findings will only add to the growing concern that the Ministry of Justice has underestimated the technical and logistical complexities of implementing a system of this scale. When questioned about the project's performance, a Ministry of Justice spokesperson refused to comment on the cost or expected completion date. With public confidence in the justice system already strained, it remains to be seen whether this beleaguered project will ever deliver on its promise. The day after the American football regular season ends has become infamous for being the busiest day of job terminations in the league. The departures of the Green Bay Packers' Mike McCarthy, the Chicago Bears' John Fox and the Atlanta Falcons' Dan Quinn left a trail of uncertainty across the league. The axing of McCarthy comes as a major shock to the Green Bay faithful, who had grown accustomed to the team's consistent success under his leadership. Despite failing to win a championship, McCarthy had established himself as one of the more respected coaches in the game, known for his no-nonsense approach and ability to get the best out of his players. The decisions came quickly on Monday morning, with each of the three teams releasing a statement confirming the news and voicing their appreciation for the departing coaches. It was a sombre day for the coaches and their families, who have dedicated their lives to working tirelessly in pursuit of NFL success. The fallout from Black Monday will continue to ripple through the league in the coming weeks, with a number of other coaching vacancies expected to be filled in the coming days. In the meantime, fans will be left to ponder the what-ifs and try to make sense of the sudden and unexpected coaching changes. Will the Packers turn to a highly sought-after young coach, or take the more experienced Matt LaFleur from Los Angeles? Plaid Cymru, the nationalist party of Wales, has become the first major party to unveil its manifesto for the upcoming Welsh Assembly election. The party's leader, Adam Price, has promised a bold and ambitious vision for a "proud, prosperous and resilient Wales". The manifesto, titled "Hapus ac Awyron" (Happy and Free in English), sets out a range of proposals aimed at tackling the key issues facing Wales, from the economy and healthcare to education and the environment. Plaid Cymru wants to hold a referendum on Welsh independence by 2025, giving the Welsh people the opportunity to decide whether to become a sovereign state. On the economy, the party promises to create a "raft of new jobs" by investing £500 million in small businesses and by giving the Welsh government control over rail fares and ownership of Wales' coastline. Price has also pledged to give the Welsh government the power to set its own interest rates, in order to make borrowing in Wales cheaper and more accessible. The UK's nuclear deterrent, Trident, is to remain a cornerstone of the country's defence strategy after a contentious Commons vote on 18 July. MPs voted 409 to 161 in favour of renewing the ageing Trident programme, which will see the replacement of the existing Vanguard-class submarines with four new Dreadnought-class vessels. The billion pound renewal programme will keep the UK at the centre of global nuclear politics for the next half century. The debate on Trident renewal has been a long and divisive one, with strong opinions on both sides of the argument. The Case Against, led by Labour's Jeremy Corbyn and the SNP's Angus Robertson, branded the renewal of the programme a waste of money that will only serve to perpetuate a "nuclear arms race" with other nations. "For more than 20 years, our Trident missile system has been the most expensive item in the Ministry of Defence budget," said Mr Corbyn, the Labour leader. "It is a relic of the Cold War, and it has no military purpose other than as a symbol of our commitment to nuclear deterrence. It is a useless and unnecessary waste of £100 billion." However, the Case For, led by Prime Minister David Cameron and Defence Secretary Michael Fallon, argued that Trident is an essential component of the UK's defence strategy and will continue to play a vital role in maintaining British interests and security. "Trident is not just a nuclear deterrent, but also a symbol of our commitment to our allies and partners around the world," said Mr Fallon. "It is a reminder that although we have moved on from the Cold War era, we still live in a world where the threat of nuclear conflict remains a reality. We cannot afford to take our eye off the ball." The decision to renew Trident follows a review by the National Audit Office (NAO), which found that the programme was meeting its affordability targets but warned that the cost could spiral out of control if delays and cost overruns continue. The Scottish National Party (SNP), which is a vocal opponent of Trident, has vowed to continue its campaign against the programme. "This is a catastrophic decision that will condemn future generations to a world of fear, nuclear proliferation and wasted public money," said Angus Robertson, the SNP's defence spokesman. The UK government will now embark on a seven-year construction programme to build the four new Dreadnought-class submarines, which will be capable of carrying up to 18 Trident missiles each.

The environment has been granted a reprieve of sorts following a series of high-profile court victories, but a new set of regulations has sparked concerns that this progress may be swiftly reversed. The new rules, which came into effect over the weekend, are part of a package of amendments to the Civil Procedure Rules (CPR), a set of guidelines that govern court proceedings in England and Wales. Prior to the changes, the rules made it relatively straightforward for individuals and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) to bring what are known as judicial reviews, or JR's, against government decisions and actions that are deemed to be causing harm to the environment. Judicial reviews, which can ultimately lead to changes being made to policies and even force government reversals, have played a significant role in high-profile cases such as Coco Beach - where a judge ruled that the £40 million project should be stopped by the courts due to lack of information, and Preston New Road, the 500-mile pipeline in the Lancashire area of England. "These new rules represent a significant step backwards for environmental justice in this country," said Brendan Lyons, a representative of Reclaim the Power. The group, which has campaigned against the fracking industry and various other environmental issues, is worried that the changes may limit the ability of individuals to challenge decisions and policies that affect them directly. "These amendments were introduced under the guise of judicial economy, but the impact is likely to be felt disproportionately by those with protected or environmental interests," added Mr Lyons. Under the changes, applicants will now be required to provide detailed legal grounds for their applications and serve court documents on those they are suing at least 28 days before the date they are to be made available to the public. Additionally, challengers will not be able to claim the costs of litigation unless they win their case outright. Proponents of the changes argue that these amendments will simply bring the UK's legal system into line with international best practice and make it easier for claims to be made through relatively normal means and channels. Some experts have expressed similar views. "This change is not unusual given that European countries apply similar principles already. But it might be a bit tougher for many claimants to achieve success,” said Kathryn Tayler, solicitor at Leigh Day, who specialise in environmental law.

The United States of America has long been known for its generous foreign aid programme, providing financial and humanitarian assistance to countries across the globe in need. According to a recent report by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), America is indeed the largest single donor of overseas aid, surpassing even the traditionally generous countries of Europe. In 2017, the United States committed a staggering $39.2 billion in overseas aid, accounting for approximately 30% of the world's total foreign aid budget. This commitment is not new, with America consistently ranking as one of the world's largest aid donors for decades. However, the country's foreign aid programme has been facing increasing scrutiny in recent years, with some arguing that its focus is misplaced or ineffective. Despite this, American foreign aid has played a significant role in supporting global development efforts, including initiatives in poverty reduction, education, and health. In particular, the US has been a key player in global responses to humanitarian crises, such as the refugee crisis in Syria and Yemen. The US government's policy shift in 2017, under the leadership of President Donald Trump, saw a reduction in the State Department's budget for diplomacy and foreign aid, sparking concerns about the future of America's overseas aid programme. However, a recent review of the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which was signed into law in 2003, has seen a significant increase in funding. In 2018, the program received its largest ever annual allocation of $6.9 billion, although there have been concerns that the plan's future was left uncertain under the new administration. For many years, the European Union has also been one of the largest donors of overseas aid, offering a combined total of over $44 billion in assistance in 2017. However, while both the US and EU have been major players in the global development landscape, the aid landscape is increasingly dominated by a growing number of emerging donors, including countries from Asia and the Middle East. China, in particular, has been stepping up its aid efforts in recent years, with commitments totalling over $2 billion to the fight against poverty and disease in Africa. Despite its commitment to overseas aid, the US continues to face criticism from within and outside government over the effectiveness and targetting of its foreign aid programme. Some argue that too much aid is being directed towards military and security programmes, with insufficient focus on long-term development and poverty reduction.

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) is the independent agency responsible for forecasting Britain's public finances. Every year they publish their outlook for the country's tax revenues and spending, and it's usually a sobering read. This year's publication is no exception. Chancellor George Osborne has made much of the fact that he has achieved his target of balancing the current budget by 2019, five years earlier than previously expected. But beneath the headlines, the OBR's forecast is less than dazzling. They expect the national debt to carry on rising, reaching 90% of GDP by 2019 - and that's the best-case scenario. The OBR also warns that Britain's economic growth is already starting to slow, and is likely to remain subdued for several years to come. "There is a real risk that things go wrong," they say. "If wages and productivity don't start growing strongly, or if there's a major trade deal or economic shock, it could all come crashing down." It's difficult to disagree with that assessment. The OBR's forecast assumes that the global economy will continue to recover, and that Britain's trade relationships will remain stable. But what if that doesn't happen? What if the dollar continues to rise, and ourexports become even less competitive? What if President Trump decides to renege on our current trade deals, and slaps tariffs on our goods? We could be back where we started, with a big budget deficit and a massive national debt. It's not a prospect that fills me with confidence. And yet, despite all these risks, the Chancellor remains upbeat. He says that his plan will unlock a new era of economic growth, and that he is confident that Britain will thrive outside the EU. It's a brave claim, but it's one that I'm afraid I don't believe. We'll have to wait and see how it all plays out, but for now, I'm not feeling quite so cheerful. The OBR's forecast may not make for pleasant reading, but at least it's a dose of reality. We need to be honest about the risks and challenges that lie ahead, not pretend that everything is going to be all right. So let's take a deep breath, and get ready for the stormy weather that may be coming our way. Britain's fiscal future is far from certain, and we need to be prepared for the worst.

Mental Health Woes Plague Northern Ireland's Healthcare In a stark revelation, it has emerged that none of the 12 health trusts in Northern Ireland is meeting the stringent waiting time targets for individuals struggling with mental health issues such as anxiety and depression. The concerning statistic has raised serious concerns about the state of mental healthcare in the region, with many calling for urgent action to address the crisis. According to the target set by the Public Health Agency (PHA), patients experiencing a range of mental health problems should receive treatment within a certain timeframe, typically within a few weeks or months, depending on the severity of their condition. However, data suggests that the vast majority of trusts are consistently failing to meet these targets, leaving countless individuals to suffer from debilitating symptoms and the distressing impact on their daily lives. "This is a stark reminder of the enduring issues with mental health services in Northern Ireland," Barry Gilbert, Chair of the regional Patient and Client Council, stated. "We have long been aware of the long waiting times, which not only delay access to treatment but also exacerbate the condition's debilitating effects on individuals and families." The PHA's waiting time target for mental health patients is to receive relevant care and treatment within a period of six weeks for the most severe conditions, 13 weeks for those with certain anxiety disorders, and 26 weeks for those with depression or post-traumatic stress disorder. However, none of the health trusts is meeting these targets, which are deemed crucial for mitigating the dire consequences of untreated mental anguish. According to PHA statistics, the worst-performing trusts saw just three in ten patients with mental health conditions receive timely treatment. In Belfast Health and Social Care Trust, only 12.5% of patients met the six-week target, while in the North West Trust, the figure was a mere 7.7%. These bleak figures underscore the magnitude of the crisis gripping Northern Ireland's mental health sector. In a bid to address the issue, the DoH and Health and Social Care (HSC) system are actively working together to develop and implement more effective workforce succession planning, improve recruitment agencies and raise staffing capacity within mental health services. There are also ongoing efforts to enhance collaboration between different health services, community groups and voluntary organisations to ensure seamless delivery of patient care and eradicate unnecessary duplication of effort.
